“There will always be water,” Amara said. “It just won’t be where you want it.”

Another child wanted to send a football. Another wanted a recording of his grandmother singing in Twi. A quiet boy with a yellow inhaler said they should send the sound of a fridge.

“Why a fridge?” Mara asked.

“Because when the power goes, you know.”

The others nodded. The fridge’s silence was a disaster signal, as clear to them as an alarm.

Mara asked whether the children thought future beings would care about human voices.

“They might not be human,” said a boy at the end.

“What would they care about, then?”

He shrugged. “Whatever they are.”

It was the most sensible answer Mara had heard all day.

Ms. Pritchard interrupted gently. “We should stay with the question.”

“That is the question,” the boy said.

Mara let the recorder continue.

A girl asked whether the people of the future would have parents. When Mara said she did not know, the girl asked how they could understand the archive without them.

“Maybe they’ll have something else,” Mara said.

“Then why are you sending them us?”

Mara had no answer prepared.

The children began talking over one another. Their answers rose and crossed: a recipe for lentil stew, the sound of rain on the conservatory roof, instructions for apologizing, a picture of the moon from the top of the estate, the words to a joke that depended on a language Mara did not speak.

One boy said they should send nothing.

“Why not?” Mara asked.

“Because if they’re happier than us, they’ll think we’re showing off.”

The teacher laughed, then covered her mouth.

Mara did not laugh. She marked the statement for transcription.

At the end of the session, Ms. Pritchard asked whether the children would receive copies.

“Of their interviews?”

“Of anything. They were told this was important.”

Mara looked at the tablet’s distribution field. Copies could be requested by participants, but processing might take six weeks. Audio would be watermarked, compressed, and held in the project’s review system until cleared for inclusion.

“I’ll make sure they get them,” she said.

It was not a promise she had authority to make.

On the way out, she found the quiet boy waiting beside the gym doors.

“My mum says the future people will be rich,” he said.

“Why?”

“Because poor people don’t get to keep things for eight million years.”

Mara looked through the glass at the gym, at the children gathering coats and inhalers and lunch containers.

“Your mum might be right,” she said.

He considered this. “Then send them something poor.”

“What?”

He held up a plastic button from his school shirt.

She almost told him the archive could not accept loose objects. Instead she asked where he had found it.

“On the floor.”

“Do you want to give it to me?”

“No. I want you to tell them it was mine.”

The housing block where the displaced families had been placed stood three miles inland, though the residents still called it temporary. The word appeared on every notice: temporary accommodation, temporary service reduction, temporary relocation, temporary limits on movement during flood alerts.

The building had once been a hotel for conference delegates. Its windows had been sealed against heat and opened only by maintenance staff. Families lived four to a room, sometimes six. The kitchens had induction plates but electricity was rationed between six and eight in the evening, so people cooked in shifts.

Mara interviewed a father who had lost his boatyard, a woman from Deptford who had not seen her sister since the evacuation, and an old man who had carried two cages of finches through waist-deep water.

Then a girl named Laleh sat before the recorder.

She was twelve, with a shaved patch above one ear where a medical sensor had been removed. She said her family had come from the coast, though she would not say which coast.

“Why not?”

“Because then you’ll make it the important part.”

Mara lowered her pen.

Laleh looked at the recorder. “Everyone asks where we came from. Nobody asks what we were doing before.”

“What were you doing?”

“Arguing with my brother about a bicycle. Learning chemistry. My aunt was making bread badly. My father had a blue shirt he hated. We had a dog that bit the postman.”

“Do you want those things included?”

“No. I want you to understand that they were there even if they aren’t useful.”

Mara thought of the archive catalogue: environmental records, genetic material, endangered languages, tools, seeds, testimony. Useful things, all of them. The project had been designed to resist disappearance, but it had not yet learned how to preserve the ordinary without turning it into evidence.

Laleh leaned toward the microphone.

“Ask me what we lost.”

“What did you lose?”

“A place where my mother knew which window got sun in winter.”

Mara waited.

“Is that enough?” Laleh asked.

“Yes.”

“But it isn’t the worst thing.”

“It doesn’t have to be the worst thing.”

Laleh studied her. “You think they’ll understand small losses?”

“I don’t know.”

“Then don’t say you’re sending them humanity. Say you’re sending them things you didn’t know how to keep.”

Mara wrote that down exactly.

By late afternoon, the recording schedule had become a machine that consumed people. Participants were offered transport vouchers, water, and a printed statement explaining the historic significance of their contribution. Most waited longer than promised. Some were too tired to speak by the time they entered the room. One man fell asleep during his own testimony and woke furious that Mara had not stopped him.

At the Continuance offices, the interview files were sorted automatically. The system assigned tags: climate displacement, labor, domestic memory, ecological grief, cultural continuity, childhood perspective. It also assigned confidence levels based on audio quality, translation certainty, and “narrative coherence.”

Tayo stared at the classification screen.

“What does that mean?” Mara asked.

“It means they prefer people who tell their suffering in a shape the software recognizes.”

“Can we remove it?”

“No.”

“Can we challenge it?”

“Yes.”

“Will that change anything?”

“It will create a record that we challenged it.”

She looked at him. “You sound like Vale.”

“I sound like someone who knows records are doors. Sometimes the only way through is to leave fingerprints.”

He had spent the day building a parallel catalogue on an old municipal server, one the project’s security team considered too obsolete to monitor. Every entry held the recording, the consent status, the interviewer’s notes, and the conditions under which the testimony had been collected.

“You’ve included the waiting times,” Mara said.

“And who paid for transport.”

“Why?”

“Because access is part of the voice.”

He opened another file. “This one is marked voluntary, but the participant came because the housing office said cooperation would help with relocation priority.”

Mara felt heat rise in her face. “She didn’t tell me that.”

“She told the intake clerk.”

“Why wasn’t it in the recording?”

“Because intake isn’t considered testimony.”

He scrolled. “This one was recruited through a university. This one through a Meridian-funded cultural trust. This one through a government resettlement office. This one through an invitation sent only to people with verified academic or professional credentials.”

“You said the estates were invited.”

“They were invited to nominate representatives.”

“Who nominated them?”

“People who had already been selected as representatives.”

Mara sat back. The office lights flickered, recovered, then dimmed to their evening setting. Somewhere below, the building’s cooling systems began shutting down in sections.

“The project wants voices,” she said.

“It wants voices that can be processed.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“No. But it can sound the same in a report.”

She opened Ruth’s file. The system had tagged her statement as infrastructure labor, public risk, and hostile language. The last category was highlighted amber.

“She said the truth.”

“The truth can be hostile.”

“To whom?”

“That’s usually the useful question.”

Mara remembered the listening room, the words she had written there beneath her identification number. We were not one thing. She had meant it as an accusation against the comfort of unity. Now the phrase seemed less stable. The people in the interviews were not one thing, but neither were their conditions. Some had been invited, some extracted, some translated badly, some made to wait until their anger cooled into something acceptable.

The following morning, Mara returned to the flood office with a second recorder.

Ruth saw it immediately.

“Is that for redundancy?”

“Yes.”

“Or because you don’t trust the first one?”

“Both.”

Ruth nodded. “Now you’re learning.”

Mara told her the project had classified parts of the testimony as hostile.

“Good,” Ruth said. “Put that in too.”

“It may not be included.”

“Then include that it may not be included.”

Mara switched on both recorders.

Ruth leaned forward, her hands clasped between her knees. “You want to know what the future should value? It should value the person who says the wall is cracking before the water comes through. It should value the person who believes them. And if it doesn’t believe them, it should at least remember the sound of being told.”

She paused.

“Do you know what we did when the barrier alarm failed?”

“No.”

“We shouted. That was the system. Thousands of people shouting into the rain.”

The sentence remained with Mara after she left.

That evening, Tayo met her on the roof of their estate. The pumps had been running since dawn, but water still glazed the lower courtyard. Across the river, the upriver towers glowed in uninterrupted bands, their private turbines turning the windows gold.

He had brought a small speaker.

“Play something,” Mara said.

“I’m not here to entertain you.”

“You brought a speaker.”

“It’s for comparing audio compression.”

He played Ruth’s recording. Her voice came through thinly at first, then sharpened: builders get statues.

The river wind took the rest and carried it toward the illuminated towers.

Tayo stopped the file. “Your interviews are already changing.”

“How?”

“Not the words. The storage paths.”

He showed her a diagram. Several files had been copied from the public intake system to a restricted review server. The system had created duplicate versions with altered metadata. In one, a participant had been changed from “displaced resident” to “urban transition witness.” In another, “evacuation refusal” had become “community adaptation.”

“Who did that?”

“Could be automated normalization. Could be a person. Could be both.”

“Can we restore the original?”

“Not in their system.”

He tapped his own catalogue. “Here, yes.”

Mara watched the duplicated files multiply across the screen, each version carrying a slightly different account of who had spoken and why.

“Maybe this is what they mean by preserving context,” she said.

Tayo smiled without amusement. “Then context is more dangerous than I thought.”

Below them, a pump coughed. The sound travelled through the building’s foundations.

Mara thought of the schoolboy’s button, Laleh’s mother’s winter window, Ruth’s shouting crews. None of them had asked to represent humanity. They had asked to remain specific.

“Future beings might not care about any of this,” she said.

“They might not care about us at all.”

“Then why keep recording?”

“Because people here care whether they were heard.”

“That isn’t the same as sending a message across eight million years.”

“No,” Tayo said. “But it may be the only part we can honestly control.”

She looked at the towers across the water, at their clean light and sealed windows. “I thought the difficult thing would be deciding what to say.”

“It’s deciding who gets to make the saying count.”

The pump below them groaned again. This time it did not recover.

Mara opened a new catalogue entry. She entered every condition she could remember: the school’s power ration, the hotel’s sealed windows, Ruth’s wet coat, the people who had declined because they could not lose a day’s wages, the ones who had spoken in languages no project translator covered, the ones who had been invited through institutions and the ones who had arrived because a notice promised priority.

Under selection notes, she typed:

The first voices were not first because they were most important. They were first because someone knew how to reach them.

She hesitated, then added:

This distinction matters.

Tayo read over her shoulder.

“Keep that,” he said.

“I am.”

“Keep the discarded ones too.”

“I don’t have them.”

“You will.”

The lights across the river brightened as the estate went dark. For a few seconds, the two sides of London appeared to belong to different planets.

Then Mara heard, below the barrier and beneath the towers, the long mechanical breathing of the city trying not to drown.

chapters.name: The Drowned Coast
chapters.content:
The first thing Mara noticed about Lagos was that the air had a taste.

Not merely heat, though heat pressed against the aircraft before the doors opened. It was salt, diesel, mud, and the sweet rot rising from blocked drains, layered together until the city seemed to be breathing through cloth.

The arrivals hall had power only in the security lanes. People stood beneath dead fans, waving printed permits and health clearances. A wall display showed a blue-green coastline beneath the words:

**COASTAL FUTURES: RESILIENT, CONNECTED, OPEN.**

The image had been taken from high above, where the water was clean enough to reflect clouds.

A driver from the Continuance delegation waited beyond the barrier with a card bearing Mara’s project number.

“Welcome,” he said.

His vehicle was electric and armoured against floodwater. As they crossed the city, Mara recorded the journey. Water occupied gutters and parts of the road. Buses, motorcycles, delivery carts, and pedestrians moved around one another in a constant negotiation. Concrete walls advertised desalination, private security, relocation bonds, and Meridian Infrastructure’s new coastal lattice.

**HOLDING THE LINE TOGETHER**, said the billboards.

Behind the seawalls, towers rose from reclaimed land, their upper levels wrapped in gardens. Beside the drainage channels, families lived beneath tarpaulins.

The driver glanced at Mara’s tablet.

“The project wants scenery?”

“It wants conditions.”

“Then record the traffic.”

“I am.”

“Record that some people can afford to be late.”

The Lagos Coastal Systems Laboratory stood behind a chain-link fence at the edge of a former research campus. A tide gauge leaned in the flooded entrance. The security guard examined Mara’s permit and called someone inside.

A woman came out wearing rubber boots, a faded yellow shirt, and a respirator hanging loose around her neck.

“Mara Venn?”

“Yes.”

“I’m Amina Bello.”

Amina led her past courtyards filled with water and abandoned laboratories. Mangrove seedlings pushed through the paving. Inside, tanks held fish, translucent jellyfish, and pale fragments of coral beneath blue lamps.

“This was a restoration facility,” Amina said. “Before restoration became an expensive word for preserving a few specimens behind glass.”

The interview room contained two chairs, a table, and a Continuance recorder. Amina placed an old scratched device beside it.

“Will I receive a copy?” she asked.

“Yes. Within six weeks, usually.”

“Use this as well.”

Mara recognized the gesture. “Redundancy.”

“Distrust,” Amina said. “Redundancy is what engineers call distrust when they want funding.”

Mara switched on both recorders.

Amina stated her name, profession, and fields of study: estuarine ecology, mangrove recovery, coral adaptation, and “the removal of dead things from places where they become poisonous.”

“Dead fish, dead birds, dead wetlands,” she said. “Dead legislation. The first three are easier to remove.”

She described shorelines moving inland by increments: a street flooded, reopened, and flooded again; a fishing village relocated behind a wall that protected a refinery rather than the village; storms arriving outside the old season; rain falling too quickly for the soil to absorb it.

“People speak of climate collapse as though the climate is a building,” she said. “As if one morning the roof falls in. Here, collapse is a sequence of permissions.”

Mara looked up.

“Permissions?”

“Someone permitted drilling in a wetland. Someone permitted a pipeline through a mangrove. Someone permitted housing on flood-storage land. Someone permitted insurers to withdraw. Someone permitted a company to spill and then settle.”

She leaned toward the recorder.

“Do not say the coast was lost. That makes it sound like an accident. The coast was taken apart. Some of it was taken for profit, some for security, some because officials wanted to appear modern. Poor people were easier to move than rich infrastructure. Everyone preferred a temporary lie to a permanent decision.”

Mara asked what the message should include.

Amina’s expression hardened.

“Not just humanity.”

“The archive includes biological samples, environmental recordings, seeds, and microbial cultures.”

“That is not what I mean.”

“We can’t interview every species.”

“No. But you can admit they were here. Preserved specimens are not witnesses.”

She opened a folder. Photographs showed mangroves blackened beneath oil, a dolphin tangled in plastic netting, a reef reduced to pale rubble, and a child standing in grey floodwater.

“Your project will send a message eight million years into the future,” she said. “You will give those beings our mathematics, music, explanations, and apologies. Where are the lives we converted into background?”

Mara said nothing.

“Name the relationships,” Amina continued. “The mangrove that held the nursery fish. The wetland that filtered water before it reached the settlement. The insects nobody catalogued because they were not useful. The shorebirds whose routes were broken by light and noise. If you preserve only what fits in a container, extinction will look tidy.”

She turned to another photograph: concrete pylons disappearing into brown water.

“Who built that?”

“A coastal protection consortium.”

“Which one?”

“Meridian Infrastructure was a primary contractor.”

“And who approved the route?”

“The Lagos coastal authority, with federal review.”

“Who financed it?”

“Multiple funds.”

“Which means no one can be named.”

Amina closed the folder. “Responsibility becomes so distributed that it evaporates. Everyone is involved; therefore no one is guilty. Your message must not do that.”

Mara wrote in the margin of her notes:

**What did they know, and when did they know it?**

After the interview, Amina took her to the rear platform overlooking the lagoon. The water had risen over the old walkway. A yellow buoy struck the railing with a hollow knock.

“The station measured salinity,” Amina said. “Now it measures whether the instruments are still above water.”

They passed tanks of young mangroves, each tagged and fitted with a sensor.

“These came from a community nursery,” Amina said. “Residents raised them after the government cleared the original mangrove belt.”

“They cleared it, then funded restoration?”

“They cleared it, built a road, watched the road flood, and hired us to restore what the road destroyed.”

“Does it work?”

“Sometimes.”

She touched a leaf. “Plants are patient. People mistake patience for consent.”

A convoy passed beyond the fence carrying modular barriers toward the peninsula.

“Where are they going?” Mara asked.

“To protect the new district.”

“And the old district?”

Amina looked toward the lagoon. “It is being described as transitional.”

That afternoon they drove to an evacuation zone north of the city. The government called it a temporary reception settlement. It had existed for four years.

Houses stood on concrete blocks. Several were marked with white numbers. At the entrance, residents crowded beneath a relocation schedule, arguing with officials in blue vests. The list was available in several languages, but many names had been misspelled.

A woman seized Amina’s arm.

“They say my name is not here.”

“You registered?”

“Three times.”

The woman produced a damp card. An official tapped through records on a tablet.

“Duplicate household,” he said.

“It is not a duplicate. My husband died.”

“Household status requires review.”

“Review where? The water is in the room.”

“The system will resolve it.”

Amina brought the woman to a desk and argued with the official in Yoruba. Mara waited until the woman agreed before recording.

“My name is Bisi Adeyemi,” she said, holding the damp card. “They have moved us three times. Each time they say it is the last move. My children know how to sleep sitting up. Do not call this resilience. We are tired.”

Behind her, a boy tried to keep a plastic boat afloat in a puddle. He had made it from a food container and a bottle cap.

Mara knelt beside him.

“What’s the boat called?”

He shrugged.

“Are you taking us somewhere?” he asked, looking at her badge.

“No. I’m recording.”

“Where will it go?”

“Into a machine.”

“Will the machine bring us back?”

“No.”

“Then why put us in it?”

“So someone knows.”

“Who?”

Mara looked at the boat tipping beneath his finger.

“I don’t know.”

Amina watched from nearby.

On the drive back, Mara asked whether the boy’s testimony should be included.

“If he consents,” Amina said. “He’s eight. His guardian must consent too.”

“Is that the only question?”

“No. Ask whether the archive will use him to make itself feel humane. A child’s fear is not automatically profound because it is small and articulate.”

Mara entered the day’s conditions in the catalogue:

**Laboratory: intermittent cooling; restricted local access. Settlement: participants recruited through relocation records; possible administrative coercion; incomplete language access. Bisi Adeyemi: consent recorded; copy promised; official household record disputed. Child, name withheld: consent pending.**

She added:

**Species and ecosystems discussed as subjects without legal or archival voice. Biologist requests preservation of relationships, not only specimens. Responsibility obscured through distributed ownership and bureaucratic language.**

Then:

**Identifiable powers: coastal authorities, federal reviewers, Meridian Infrastructure, financing bodies, security agencies, project administrators. People who signed. People who knew. People who profited. People who called it temporary.**

Amina was looking through the window at the wet city.

“Did you always believe the warnings?” Mara asked.

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because I believed them and did nothing.”

Mara turned toward her.

“When I was twenty-five, I saw the projections. I thought there would be time. Then I got a grant, then a better position. My work became adaptation because mitigation was politically offensive. We learned to breed fish that tolerated polluted water instead of asking why the water was polluted.”

“Were you responsible?”

“For some things.”

“Isn’t that what everyone says? That they were only one part of it?”

“Yes. That is why I’m careful about what I claim.”

The driver slowed at a checkpoint. Armed guards examined the vehicle and waved it through.

Amina said, “Your mother understood this.”

Mara’s breath caught. “You knew her?”

“Not well. We met at a coastal systems conference in Accra. She was furious.”

“That sounds like her.”

“She said models were being used as weather forecasts for investors. If the numbers frightened people with power, they were called uncertain. If the same numbers protected an insurance market, they were called actionable.”

“Did she talk about Continuance?”

“She hated the way people used it. That is not the same as hating the project.”

“What did she think the message should say?”

Amina watched the rain gather on the glass.

“Something that would make the future uncomfortable. She said the future should know the sea was not an enemy. We made it carry everything we did not want to see.”

Back at the laboratory, Amina gave Mara photographs, mangrove data, and a list of species documented in the lagoon before the last dredging project. Several entries ended with question marks. Others had only local names.

“Will these be accepted?” Mara asked.

“Ask them.”

Mara transferred the files. The system required a classification. The categories included ecological loss, climate displacement, and cultural continuity, but not destruction by named policy or species without taxonomic confirmation. She selected **OTHER**.

A warning appeared:

**OTHER MATERIALS MAY EXPERIENCE DELAYED REVIEW.**

Mara accepted.

“Your machine has a gentle way of saying no,” Amina said.

“Not yet.”

“Not yet is how it begins.”

That night, the delegation housed Mara in a tower hotel above the protected district. The room had filtered air, sealed windows, and uninterrupted electricity. Below, floodlights illuminated the seawall. Beyond it, darkness spread over the lagoon.

She listened to the recordings: Ruth’s voice, the children in the gymnasium, Laleh describing the winter sun, Bisi saying, *We are tired*, and Amina saying, *The coast was taken apart.*

Mara opened her draft.

**We were not one thing.**

She added:

**We were not alone in the world, though we often behaved as if naming a thing gave us the right to use it. The sea carried our waste, our ships, our heat, and our dead. Wetlands held back water until we built over them. Fish bred in waters we poisoned. Birds changed their routes beneath our lights. Some lives we damaged had names. Some had only the names given by those who watched them disappear. Do not mistake our failure to record them for their absence.**

She continued:

**Ask who decided. Ask who knew. Ask who gained time, land, safety, or profit. Ask who was moved and who was protected. Ask who called destruction adaptation because the truthful word would have required action.**

The paragraph felt too smooth. Amina would object to its confidence. Ruth would object to its distance. The boy with the plastic boat might ask where the machine was taking it.

Mara saved the draft under C-417, then under a second name: **LAGOON_RAW_01**.

She sent the second file to Tayo’s catalogue.

The transfer icon turned red, then green.

His reply arrived:

**Received. Keeping original conditions.**

A second message followed:

**You sound angry.**

Mara looked at the seawall, built to protect a future that had already decided whom it could leave behind.

She typed:

**I am trying not to sound certain.**

Tayo answered:

**Those are different problems.**

Rain blurred the lights until the city looked submerged already. Mara placed Amina’s species list beside the project tablet. At the bottom, one entry had been written by hand:

*Unknown mangrove insect, locally called the dusk needle. Not seen since dredging, 2041.*

Mara did not know whether the insect had mattered to the mangrove, the fish, or the people who had given it a name. She knew only that someone had noticed its absence and written it down.

She added the line to the archive.

Then she began again.

**We were not one thing. But nothing we harmed was only one thing either.**

chapters.name: The House That Moves
chapters.content:
The House That Moves

Jakarta appeared first as a brightness beneath cloud.

From the aircraft, Mara saw her own face reflected over scattered lights. Between them lay broad black areas where power had been rationed, streets had flooded, or the city had decided darkness was cheaper than repair. The sea was not visible, though she imagined its pressure beneath the fuselage.

On the ground, the air smelled of salt, hot metal, rain trapped in drains, and vegetation left too long underwater.

A Meridian liaison met her at the terminal with a sign bearing the Continuance seal and her project number.

“C-417,” he said, checking her face against his tablet.

“Mara is fine.”

He smiled as if she had made a joke. “Of course.”

The terminal screens showed a blue-green animation of the new coastal lattice: walls, pumps, floating transit corridors, neighborhoods rising above the flood line. Beneath it appeared: COORDINATED ADAPTATION IS SHARED SURVIVAL.

There were no people carrying mattresses through brown water. No children sleeping in schools. No one waiting for a pump to restart.

The liaison introduced himself as Arif and led her through security to a vehicle with glare-treated windows. They moved slowly through streets shining after rain.

They stopped after twelve minutes.

A barrier had lowered across the road. Beyond it, motorcycles stood half-submerged in an intersection where the asphalt had become a shallow lake. A woman in a yellow rain cape carried a sleeping child above the water.

Arif tapped his tablet. “The route has been adjusted.”

“Because of the flood?”

“Because of congestion.”

Mara looked at the water reaching the doors of a closed pharmacy. “What do you call this?”

He gave the careful answer. “Temporary disruption within managed parameters.”

The language arrived before the failure, as if naming it incorrectly could keep it from becoming real.

They left the vehicle and followed a raised footway toward the school. It had once been a primary school; now its lower floors held a cooling center and emergency records office. Classes were held upstairs when there was power.

The teacher waiting for Mara was Sari Wibowo. She wore a green headscarf and carried keys clipped to her belt. Behind her, twenty-three children sat on woven mats beneath a stopped ceiling fan.

“The fan is ornamental now,” Sari said. “It reminds them that air used to move by itself.”

Some children laughed. Others stared at Mara’s recorder.

Sari had agreed to speak only if the children remained. She did not want to be taken away from them and turned into an isolated representative of a place she could not leave. The consent form called her an educator and climate-displacement witness. She had crossed out witness and written teacher.

“I am not here because I survived a flood,” she told Mara. “I am here because I taught children while the flood was happening.”

The room smelled of chalk, wet clothes, and algae from a bucket beneath a leaking window.

Sari described the school’s changing timetable. Lessons moved to dawn during hot months, then to evenings when the grid failed. Science classes became evacuation drills. Geography became an argument over which maps remained accurate. Three children stopped attending after their families were moved to a tower complex. One girl returned after two months and no longer remembered which classroom was hers.

“Do you record attendance?” Mara asked.

“Every day.”

“Does the archive include that?”

“The archive includes the percentage of children maintained in education during displacement.” Sari’s mouth tightened. “It does not include that Dimas slept under his desk because he was afraid to go home. Or that Nuri’s father disappeared after refusing to sign the relocation agreement. Or that children attended because school was the only place with clean water.”

“What would you want future beings to know?”

Sari looked toward the children. “That we kept teaching.”

It was the answer Mara had expected and distrusted.

“Why?”

The children grew quiet.

“Because they were there,” Sari said.

“That explains duty. Not hope.”

“Do you think teaching is hope?”

“I think people call many things hope after the fact.”

Sari smiled without amusement. “Your mother asked questions like that.”

Mara’s hand tightened around the recorder.

“You knew Leila?”

“Once. At a conference. She spoke about coastal models and the danger of using uncertainty as permission to delay.” Sari turned her keys around one finger. “Afterward, she came to our school. She wanted to know what maps meant to the children inside them. The officials were unhappy.”

“What did she say?”

“That normal was not a direction.”

The words altered the room. Mara had heard them at home years ago, when her mother was alive and the kitchen window had not been sealed against bad air.

Sari continued. “She said a map could be accurate and still cruel if it showed a future without showing the people required to endure it.”

Mara looked at the children.

“Do not make my school into a lesson about courage,” Sari said.

“What should it be?”

“A school.”

The interview lasted forty-seven minutes. Sari spoke of children sleeping through pump alarms, parents moving their homes one room at a time to higher floors, and lessons beside emergency charging stations. She recorded a song the children sang while carrying books upstairs. They sang badly and loudly. When the power returned, the fan began turning without cooling the room.

At the end, Sari asked whether she would receive a copy.

“Within six weeks,” Mara said. “The local version may be compressed and watermarked.”

“Will it contain my corrections?”

“If they preserve the original.”

“And if they do not?”

Mara hesitated.

“Then record that I asked.”

Mara did.

That evening, Arif took her to a Meridian hospitality tower overlooking the old shoreline. The building stood on a raised platform protected by a private barrier. From the dining room, Mara saw submerged margins glittering beneath floodlights: towers, cranes, warning beacons, maintenance drones.

Her room had filtered air, uninterrupted electricity, and a bed that adjusted itself when she lay down. She sent Tayo the day’s files through the protected channel.

**Teacher rejects witness classification. Says school is not a lesson.**

His reply came eleven minutes later.

**Good. Lessons are usually where institutions hide the bodies. Your Jakarta location metadata has been normalized. Original copy preserved.**

**How?**

**Not yet. Sleep if possible.**

She did not sleep. Rain struck the window so hard that she imagined the glass failing. She thought of the school’s children beneath the stopped fan, and of the probe traveling beyond the planets with their song sealed inside it.

In the morning she flew west.

The settlement outside Athens had been built around an abandoned logistics depot, though its official name was the Transitional Inland Reception Community of Nea Phylaki. The perimeter fence was new. The warehouses were old. Between them stood rows of modular homes with white roofs and wheels that had never touched the ground.

Mara’s driver said the wheels were required by regulation.

“For relocation,” he explained.

“Have any moved?”

“Some units have.”

“Those units?”

He looked toward the settlement. “The designation does not guarantee mobility.”

Wind carried dust across the road. Solar panels angled toward a pale sun. Children watched a water truck enter through the gate.

The families had been selected by a resettlement organization funded by governments and Meridian foundations. Their consent forms were available in several languages. One woman told Mara the form had been explained in a language she only partly understood, and that she had signed because refusing could delay her housing transfer.

“Voluntary,” the coordinator said when Mara asked.

“Under what conditions?”

“Participation has no bearing on eligibility.”

A woman named Dalia laughed from the doorway of her unit. “Everything has bearing on eligibility.”

Dalia had come from Alexandria with her two daughters and her brother’s family. The sea had entered their neighborhood twice in one year. The third time, authorities demolished the lower floors and marked the buildings for clearance. Her husband had died before the relocation, and his name remained on several documents while being absent from the one that mattered.

“We are six people in a home designed for four,” she said. “The software says five because my brother’s youngest is registered under his dead mother.”

“Have you appealed?”

“Three times.”

“And?”

“The appeal is being reviewed.”

“Since when?”

“Before the last winter.”

Her daughter brought out three pale oranges from the morning distribution. Dalia cut one with a small knife and gave the pieces to the children, keeping none.

“What do you want future beings to know?”

Dalia considered the recorder. “A home is not the walls.”

“What is it?”

“Knowing where the light will be in winter. Knowing which neighbor has medicine. Knowing whose roof leaks and who will come with a bucket. Knowing where the dead are buried.”

She told Mara the settlement had electricity and clean water most days. It was safer than the place she had left. She did not want the record to turn that fact into gratitude.

“Safety is not belonging,” she said. “But do not erase safety because it is insufficient. We need both.”

In other units, a family from the Sundarbans described losing a village to a river that moved through it over six seasons. A young man from Tripoli said the settlement gave him a roof but no future because his employment permit remained pending. A woman from Thessaloniki said she had lived in the warehouse district for eight years and did not know whether she counted as displaced or merely poor.

Every testimony resisted the categories waiting for it.

At the settlement’s edge, children had built a playground from shipping pallets. Mara found Sami sitting beneath one of the units, drawing on the back of a food-distribution notice.

He was perhaps nine, with unevenly cut black hair and a red coat too large for him.

“Can I see?”

He turned the paper around.

It showed a small house with four wheels, two windows, and a blue door. Behind it were green hills and a yellow sun with a serious face.

“Does it drive?” Mara asked.

“Yes.”

“Where does it go?”

“Anywhere the water is not.”

“Does it have an engine?”

“No. Houses do not need engines.”

“Then how does it move?”

“People move it.”

He added two figures beside the house, then a dog with enormous ears.

“Is this your home?”

“It is the home after.”

“After what?”

“After we get a home.”

“Where is your home now?”

He pointed to the units. “There.”

“And before?”

“There was another.”

“Do you remember it?”

“I remember the stairs.”

“What about them?”

“They went up to my room. The new place has no stairs.”

“Do you miss it?”

He pressed the pencil into the paper until it tore. “My mother says missing places is not useful.”

“Is she right?”

He looked at Mara. “Are you making a message for the future?”

“Yes.”

“What will they do with it?”

“I don’t know.”

“Can they send things back?”

“No.”

“Can they send houses?”

“No.”

“Can they send water?”

Mara had no prepared answer.

Sami folded the drawing along the roofline. “Then why do you send it?”

“Because someone may find it.”

“Who?”

“People who live a long time from now.”

“Will they be people?”

“We don’t know.”

“Then why should they care about us?”

The question held no anger. That made it harder.

Mara thought of the probe beneath Greenwich, of the children singing in Jakarta, of Laleh’s warning not to claim she was sending humanity, only things they had not known how to keep.

“Maybe they should not,” Mara said.

Sami frowned.

“Maybe they do not owe us care. But if they find us, they should know we were here. Not as an excuse. Not as proof that everything we did was necessary.”

“Why would they want to know?”

“Because they might make mistakes too.”

“Then they should know the mistakes before they make them.”

“Yes.”

“Did people know before?”

Mara looked at the folded drawing.

“Some did.”

“Why didn’t they stop?”

“Because knowing is not the same as choosing.”

He seemed dissatisfied. He unfolded the paper and drew a long black line beside the house, with smaller lines branching from it.

“What is that?”

“A road.”

“It looks like water.”

“It is both.”

He handed her the drawing. “Keep it if you want. But don’t put it in the machine if the machine cannot make a house.”

Mara took it.

That night, she sat in the settlement office while the coordinator uploaded the interviews. A warning appeared beside Sami’s file: MINOR—IDENTITY AND GUARDIAN CONSENT INCOMPLETE. Mara did not attach the drawing. She scanned it separately and entered no name, only **CHILD’S DRAWING, NEA PHYLAKI, HOUSE WITH WHEELS**.

She opened a new document.

**The future is not an audience to which we are entitled.**

The sentence looked severe. She left it.

**We imagined you because we were unable to protect everyone living beside us. This may be vanity. It may also be fear: the fear that what happened would disappear if no one carried it forward.**

She stopped. Sari’s voice returned: Do not make my school into a lesson about courage.

Mara deleted the second paragraph and began again.

**There were children who learned the names of flood barriers before the names of trees. There were teachers who taught during blackouts, families who moved from one temporary home to another, and children who drew houses with wheels because a fixed house could no longer be trusted. Do not mistake these things for our goodness. They are records of what was required of us, and of what we failed to provide.**

She read it twice. It was accurate, but too clean.

She added:

**A safe room did not replace a lost home. A functioning pump did not absolve the people who had allowed the water to rise. Improvement mattered. It was never the whole account.**

Outside, the settlement lights dimmed in sections. One row went dark, then another. Somewhere beyond the office wall, a child began crying. An adult murmured until the crying softened.

Mara placed Sami’s drawing beside the recorder. The house seemed to lean into the wind, its wheels pointed toward a road that was also water.

Tayo’s protected channel pulsed.

**How was Athens?**

She typed:

**A boy asked why the future should care. I couldn’t answer without making the future into a judge.**

His reply appeared.

**Maybe it doesn’t have to care. Maybe it has to know what it inherits.**

Mara looked at the sentence, then at the dark settlement beyond the glass.

She had thought the probe’s moral purpose was to persuade the future that humanity had been worth saving. Sari had refused to become evidence of courage. Dalia had refused to be grateful for half a home. Sami had refused to offer his drawing to a machine that could not return anything.

The project promised continuity. But continuity could be another word for asking the injured to make themselves useful to the distant and powerful.

She opened the catalogue and entered a new note:

**Future beings may not owe us admiration, pity, or forgiveness. The question is whether we owe them an account that does not turn their existence into our reward.**

Then she attached the drawing to the private file, not the official one.

For now, it was the only place she knew to put a house that moved.

chapters.name: The Weight of Continuity
chapters.content:
Kyoto received them under a sky the color of wet paper.

The delegation arrived by night, when the heat was less dangerous and the city’s cooling quota had not yet tightened. From the train, Mara saw temple roofs emerging between towers of emergency housing, their black tiles shining with recent rain. Along the elevated road, blue Meridian signs repeated the same sentence in Japanese, English, and Mandarin:

**COORDINATED ADAPTATION IS SHARED SURVIVAL.**

The letters appeared on flood pumps, medical depots, ration kiosks, and the walls of a school whose lower windows had been sealed against smoke. A second line followed on some signs:

**PRESERVING WHAT CONNECTS US.**

Mara looked away before the slogan could become scenery.

Their accommodation was a former hotel near the Kamo River, converted into an international residence for Continuance delegates. The river ran high beneath its bridges. Temporary flood gates stood stacked beside the embankment like pale teeth. Across the water, paper lanterns hung outside a restaurant that served algae broth, imported rice, and, for those with the correct access tier, real fish.

Dr. Binta Adeyemi had warned Mara that the Kyoto consultations would be more difficult than the interviews in Lagos or Nea Phylaki.

“People here have had longer to think about preservation,” she said as they crossed the lobby. “That does not mean they agree about what deserves preserving.”

Mara’s badge—**C-417**—pulled at the collar of her shirt. It seemed designed to make her feel both important and replaceable.

“Do they know I’m seventeen?” she asked.

“They know your age.”

“Then why do they keep calling me the human representative?”

“Because representatives are easier to argue with than institutions.”

Binta smiled, but not comfortably.

The first session took place in a renovated archive hall behind a temple complex that had survived three floods, two fires, and the conversion of the surrounding district into a climate refuge zone. Its old wooden beams had been reinforced with carbon lattice. Dehumidifiers murmured beneath painted screens. The room smelled of cedar, dust, and the faint medicinal sharpness of sterilized paper.

At the far end stood a conservation chamber containing scrolls, tablets, woven prayer strips, and a sealed cabinet of pre-digital storage. On the wall, a display explained that the oldest manuscripts had survived because generations of people had copied them by hand.

Mara thought of the six memory crystals beneath Greenwich, each capable of holding more words than any living person could read.

The Kyoto host was an archivist named Tomoe Ishikawa. She was small, silver-haired, and moved with the deliberateness of someone accustomed to lifting fragile objects. Her left hand trembled when she poured tea, though she did not spill any.

“Your project uses the word continuity,” Ishikawa said. “It is a beautiful word. That is why it should alarm you.”

No one laughed. The delegates had learned, over the previous weeks, that Ishikawa’s warnings arrived dressed as courtesy.

She led Mara through a side gallery where visitors could see the archive’s working rooms through glass. Conservators in pale coats repaired paper with brushes finer than eyelashes. One woman held a fragment beneath magnification while another compared it with a digital image projected on the wall.

“Continuity is never simply what survives,” Ishikawa said. “It is what someone decides must be carried forward. That decision creates a burden. Sometimes it creates a weapon.”

Mara glanced at the old scrolls. “You think the probe is a weapon?”

“I think a civilization may be destroyed by believing its continuity matters more than anything else.”

The sentence settled between them.

Ishikawa explained that one of the archive’s most valuable collections had belonged to a court whose rulers claimed to preserve the nation through ritual. They copied laws, genealogies, poems, agricultural records. They also destroyed records that contradicted the official line of succession.

“The court survived for centuries,” she said. “Then it did not. Its continuity was treated as sacred. People were sacrificed to maintain it. When the structure finally failed, those sacrifices were described as necessary, and the description became part of the inheritance.”

“Is that what you think we’re doing?” Mara asked.

“You have a vessel. You have a return date. You have chosen a future and called it a witness.” Ishikawa’s eyes rested on Mara’s badge. “You may be preserving evidence. You may also be asking the future to confirm that the people who built the vessel were important.”

Mara thought of Sami’s drawing, folded inside the lining of her bag. A house with wheels. A road that looked like water. A dog.

“We don’t know what they’ll think.”

“Then do not instruct them.”

The phrase sounded like Vale, though Ishikawa had never met him.

In the consultation hall, the first argument concerned beauty.

Professor Hana Sato, an artist who worked with living pigments and flood-damaged textiles, presented a sequence of images for the archive: a girl’s hand under rain, a cracked bowl repaired with copper, an algae bloom seen from orbit, a neighborhood market at dusk. She wanted the visual collection to be large enough that future beings could understand humans had not lived by data alone.

“If they find measurements without tenderness,” Sato said, “they will mistake us for a species that only calculated its own extinction.”

A representative from the Meridian Cultural Ministry objected that tenderness was difficult to authenticate and impossible to rank.

“That is precisely why it belongs there,” Sato replied.

The legal adviser from the European Continuity Council tapped his tablet. “The archive cannot become an anthology of private sentiment. We need coherent categories.”

“Coherent for whom?” Sato asked.

“For retrieval.”

“For obedience,” she said.

The translation system softened the exchange. On Mara’s screen, Sato’s words appeared as: **For institutional compliance.**

Mara raised her hand.

Everyone turned toward her with an attention that was not respect exactly, but the anticipation of a useful disturbance.

“The images need their conditions attached,” she said. “Who made them. Who was excluded. What equipment was available. What was destroyed before the image was taken.”

Sato looked at her with sudden interest.

Mara continued. “A photograph of a restored wetland should include the road that was built through it, the species that didn’t return, and the people moved away from it. But that doesn’t mean we shouldn’t include the photograph.”

“Beauty with an indictment attached,” said the legal adviser.

“Beauty with its circumstances attached.”

He frowned as if circumstances were a form of contamination.

The second argument concerned salvation.

A Buddhist delegate named Reverend Kaito spoke from behind a plain wooden table. He had refused the ceremonial robes offered by the host committee and wore a gray jacket with a small stain on one cuff. He argued that the archive should include prayers, burial customs, meditations, and records of mercy because a message to the far future should acknowledge the possibility that existence was not a contest for permanence.

A Christian theologian from Nairobi agreed, though she wanted the archive to include confession and judgment.

A Hindu scholar from Chennai warned against reducing every tradition to a single principle of salvation. A Muslim historian from Fez said that the archive must record not only religious belief but the politics done in its name. A secular philosopher from São Paulo asked whether salvation was merely another word for wanting to be excused.

“People who are dying need more than an inventory of their errors,” Reverend Kaito said.

“People who are being killed often receive prayers instead of protection,” the historian answered.

The room tightened.

Mara remembered Laleh describing the blue shirt she hated, Dalia explaining winter light, Sari saying that teaching was what duty required. None of them had spoken about redemption. They had spoken about bread, windows, children, pumps, names missing from forms.

A panelist asked Mara whether she believed the archive should offer hope.

She looked down at her notes. The official template contained a field marked **EMOTIONAL ORIENTATION: OPTIMISTIC / CAUTIONARY / MIXED**.

“I don’t know what hope means if it can be selected from a menu,” she said.

Someone shifted in their chair.

“Hope is not a mood,” she continued. “It might be a practice. Or a promise. But if we include it, we should include the conditions under which people were expected to hope. Who was asked to endure? Who was told that patience was a virtue while someone else received the barrier, the power, the clean water?”

Reverend Kaito studied her. “And do you think faith should be preserved?”

“I think people’s faith should be preserved if they consented to it. I don’t think we should make faith explain everything.”

“Nor suffering?”

“Especially not suffering.”

Afterward, the theologian found Mara beside the tea station.

“You are cautious with redemption,” she said.

“I’m cautious with anything that makes an ending sound deserved.”

The woman nodded slowly. “That is not the same as rejecting it.”

“No,” Mara said. “But I don’t know if we have earned the right to promise it.”

The woman lifted a cup and watched steam gather against its rim. “Perhaps redemption is not something the dead earn.”

Mara thought of her mother, though she tried not to. “Then who does?”

The theologian did not answer.

That evening, Mara walked alone along the Kamo River. The delegation had been invited to a reception, but she could not bear another room where people spoke about humanity as if it were a committee with a shared opinion. The river carried branches, wrappers, and one yellow child’s sandal beneath the bridge.

On the opposite bank, people had gathered for a festival relocated from a district that flooded every summer. Lanterns floated in shallow trays. Some were made of paper; others were printed polymer, waterproof and reusable. A speaker announced that the event honored the endurance of cultural memory.

Mara wondered what the festival would have been called if the district had not been evacuated.

Her phone vibrated. Tayo.

**Did Kyoto improve you?**

She sent back a picture of the river.

**It has not yet consented to being an archive.**

His reply took a minute.

**Good. Rivers are terrible witnesses. No narrative coherence.**

She smiled despite herself.

Then he wrote:

**Board uploaded new retrieval model. Beauty scores high. Ordinary life scores “low differentiation.”**

Mara stopped walking.

**What does that mean?**

**It means a thousand people cooking rice are less valuable than one speech about civilization.**

She watched a lantern spin in an eddy until its flame went out.

**Can you preserve the old model?**

**Already did. Protected copy. Also, your Jakarta file. Original location data attached. Don’t tell anyone I’m becoming sentimental.**

**You are becoming a criminal.**

**The distinction is administrative.**

She put the phone away, but Tayo’s message remained in her mind: low differentiation.

The next morning, an artists’ roundtable met beneath a ceiling painted with clouds. The participants had been asked to propose “representative forms of human beauty.” Their answers made representation sound like a hostile territory.

A composer wanted lullabies, work songs, traffic rhythms, mourning chants, and the vibration of buildings under wind. A sculptor argued for tools and hands rather than finished monuments. A filmmaker wanted footage of ordinary rooms—kitchens, bedrooms, clinics, buses—because grand architecture showed what societies wanted to be seen as, not how people lived.

A poet from Seoul said the archive should contain jokes that failed in translation.

“Why?” asked a government delegate.

“Because failure is a form of information.”

The delegate looked offended. “Humor can inflame ethnic tensions.”

“So can history.”

Mara wrote that down.

Professor Sato projected an image of a flooded shopping center. Fish moved through the upper levels. The photograph was beautiful, almost unbearably so. A soft green light entered through the broken roof. In the distance, a mannequin wore a red coat.

“This image has already been used in three official campaigns,” Sato said. “One called it evidence of ecological recovery. Another called it proof of infrastructure resilience. A third used it to sell insurance.”

“Then it should be excluded,” said the legal adviser.

“Because it has been misused?”

“Because its meaning is compromised.”

Sato turned to Mara. “What do you think?”

Mara stared at the mannequin’s blank face.

“Include the image,” she said. “Include every known use of it. Include the photographer’s statement. Include the flooded district’s records. Include the names of species identified in the water, if they’re known. Include the fact that people argued about what it meant.”

The legal adviser sighed. “At that rate, every object will require an archive of its own.”

“Maybe it does.”

The room went quiet. In the silence, Mara heard the dehumidifiers, the scrape of a chair, the soft electrical tick of the translation units.

She had arrived in Kyoto assuming contradiction was a weakness. A message could be challenged by too many voices, delayed by too many qualifications, made unreadable by the effort to preserve every condition. Vale had told her not to speak for a unified humanity, but she had understood that as a demand for honesty. Now she wondered whether honesty itself might require admitting that no account could stand alone.

Beauty without damage was propaganda.

Damage without beauty was another kind of lie.

Faith could comfort and excuse. Mathematics could reveal and conceal. Ordinary life could humanize suffering, but it could also make systems disappear behind the intimacy of a kitchen.

That afternoon, Ishikawa took her to a storage room where the temperature was kept just above freezing. Shelves held boxes labeled in languages Mara could not read.

“These are records recovered after the northern fires,” Ishikawa said. “Many were damaged beyond interpretation. Some contain only lists of names. Some contain arguments about whether the names are complete.”

“Are incomplete lists useful?”

“Are complete lists possible?”

Mara touched the edge of a box but did not lift it.

Ishikawa said, “A younger archivist once told me our purpose was to preserve the past. I asked him which past. He said, ‘The one that happened.’”

“That sounds reasonable.”

“It is a dangerous answer. What happened is not a single object waiting to be placed on a shelf. It is an arrangement of bodies, records, omissions, weather, power, memory, and later decisions.”

Mara thought of Bisi’s duplicate household. A dead husband present in one system and absent in another. A child’s fear waiting for guardian consent. A dusk needle recorded as “unknown,” still possibly living somewhere beyond the dredged lagoon.

“Then what is the archivist’s purpose?”

“To keep the record from becoming too easy.”

Ishikawa opened a box. Inside were thin strips of paper, each marked with a name and a date. Some had been crossed out. Some had been added later in different ink.

“Civilizations like smooth stories,” she said. “Beginnings, disasters, recovery, continuation. But people do not live inside smooth stories. They live in interruptions.”

Mara looked at the names.

“Does preserving contradiction ever stop people from acting?”

“Yes,” Ishikawa said. “If they use complexity as an excuse for paralysis. But the answer is not to simplify the record. The answer is to act without pretending the record is simple.”

That night Mara opened a new file.

The heading in the project system read:

**MESSAGE STRUCTURE: HUMAN CONTRIBUTION TO COSMIC CONTINUITY**

She deleted it.

In its place she typed:

**WE WERE NOT ONE THING.**

Then, beneath the words, she began a list.

A prayer for the dead, and the record of a government that delayed their rescue.

A mathematical proof, and the names of those who were denied schooling.

A song carried upstairs during a flood, and the statistics that counted the school as operational.

A photograph of fish swimming through a department store, and the contracts that made the flood profitable.

A recipe, a warning, a joke that failed translation.

A child’s drawing of a house with wheels, held outside the official archive because consent was incomplete.

She paused over the last line. Sami had not wanted his drawing put in a machine that could not make a house. She would not violate that instruction. But she could record the fact that it existed, and why it had been kept apart.

Mara added:

**Some things were withheld not because they lacked value, but because value did not cancel consent.**

She read the sentence again.

For the first time, the archive did not seem to her like a monument waiting to be completed. It seemed more like a room in which incompatible people had been asked to remain present while the walls shifted around them.

Outside, Kyoto’s rain began again. Water moved through old channels beneath new streets. Somewhere beyond the residence, temple bells sounded the hour, each note fading before the next arrived.

Mara saved the file in three places: the official directory, her private device, and the protected channel Tayo had built.

Then she added a catalogue note:

**Contradiction is not evidence that a record has failed. Sometimes it is the record of who was allowed to matter.**

chapters.name: The Owners of Memory
chapters.content:
## The Owners of Memory

The first claim arrived in a box lined with grey foam.

It was delivered to Continuance at nine in the morning by two men from Meridian Biologics, though neither man wore that name on his badge. Their badges displayed only the company’s white compass: four arrows pointing toward a centre that was not marked.

The box contained a seed.

Mara knew this because Dr. Sanaa El-Khatib opened it beneath a hood of filtered air and because the seed had been photographed from six angles before anyone was permitted to touch it. It was black, ridged, and no larger than a fingernail clipping. Its label read:

**MANGROVE TAXON—COASTAL STABILISATION LINE—PROPERTY OF MERIDIAN BIOLOGICS**

“Property?” Mara asked.

The two men stood behind Sanaa, expressionless in their identical charcoal jackets.

“Licensed biological material,” said the taller one. “Property is the legally operative term in the relevant jurisdictions.”

“It grew on a coast,” Mara said.

“It was sequenced, modified, and preserved by our laboratories.”

“Was it yours before that?”

The shorter man smiled as though she had asked whether a machine belonged to the person who had invented the screwdriver. “Continuance would not exist without private investment.”

Sanaa kept her eyes on the seed. “The archive was not presented to us as a commercial repository.”

“It is not a repository,” the taller man said. “It is a protected transmission. Protection requires ownership.”

Outside the laboratory, the building’s ventilation gave a long, tired shudder. A warning light blinked above the door. The city had entered its afternoon power ration, two hours earlier than scheduled.

Mara looked through the observation glass at the biological archive: racks of sealed cultures, seed capsules, fungal samples, pollen, fragments of tissue held in suspension. Labels multiplied across the cold white shelves. Some names were scientific. Some were local names, translated three times. Amina’s dusk needle was not in this room. It remained in a provisional category called OTHER, awaiting review.

“What exactly are you claiming?” Mara asked.

The taller man unfolded a tablet. “The right to determine access, replication, sequencing, modification, and contextual presentation of materials developed through Meridian-funded research.”

“Contextual presentation.”

“Who is permitted to describe them. Under what terms. With what attribution.”

“And if future beings receive the archive?”

“Then future beings receive materials that are not falsely represented as ownerless.”

The seed lay between them in its dish.

Mara thought of the village behind the refinery wall in Lagos, of mangroves cut away to make room for storage yards and private roads. She thought of Amina saying that the coast had been taken apart through a sequence of permissions. It seemed the sequence had continued into the future: first the living thing, then the laboratory, then the label.

“Does Meridian own the air around it?” Mara asked.

The shorter man’s smile disappeared. “This tone is not useful.”

“Neither is pretending a seed applied for a patent.”

Sanaa turned off the hood light. The seed vanished into reflection.

“We will review the wording,” she said.

The taller man nodded. “We expect a written response by Friday.”

After they left, Sanaa sealed the box and carried it toward cold storage.

“Will it go in?” Mara asked.

“I don’t know.”

“Because it belongs to them?”

“Because they may refuse permission.”

“It’s a seed.”

“It is also a revenue stream, a patent family, a bargaining instrument, and proof of technical leadership.” Sanaa tapped the box with one gloved finger. “The future may be interested in all of those things. The question is whether we are allowed to say so.”

Mara wrote the question in her notebook.

At noon, the board convened an emergency editorial session.

The board room had no windows, though an entire wall displayed a live projection of the Greenwich parkland. The trees were always shown in summer, green and unthreatened. On the table sat three flag cards, five corporate emblems, and a bowl of fruit imported from a region whose reservoirs had been placed under emergency restriction.

Dr. Anika Rao opened the meeting by apologising for the delay.

“The delay,” said the legal adviser, “is a consequence of increased participation.”

“Participation” had become the preferred term for demands.

Three governments had submitted revisions to the climate testimony. The Coastal Federation objected to “barrier negligence.” The Northern Compact objected to “managed sacrifice zones.” The Republic of Cascadia objected to an interview in which a fisherman described a state relocation programme as “eviction with forms.”

“Those descriptions are emotionally charged,” the adviser said. “They imply intentionality where the records support complexity.”

Ruth Ankomah’s face appeared on the wall projection. She sat in a flood-response depot, her coat still wet, and spoke about a drowned boy whose name she had never learned.

“Who stood behind the walls?” Ruth asked in the recording. “What did they know, and when did they know it?”

The legal adviser paused the image.

“The phrase ‘stood behind the walls’ has been interpreted as an accusation against protected districts,” he said. “We recommend replacing it with ‘differential exposure during emergency adaptation.’”

Mara felt the old anger rise, clean and immediate.

“That is not a replacement,” she said. “It removes the people from the sentence.”

“It makes the sentence retrievable across languages.”

“It makes it harmless.”

Professor Binta Adeyemi leaned forward. “The speaker specifically requested that the classification ‘hostile language’ remain attached to her record.”

“Yes,” said the adviser. “But classification is an internal processing term. It need not be transmitted.”

“Why not?”

“Because it may suggest that Continuance endorses antagonistic framing.”

Binta’s hand tightened around her pen. “It may suggest that someone called her hostile.”

“Which is precisely the sort of institutional dispute that will make participation impossible.”

Mara looked at the flags. The Coastal Federation’s representative had submitted a statement about shared resilience. The statement mentioned rising seas but not the decisions that had directed pumps, barriers, loans, and relocation corridors. It described the flood as a challenge encountered by all.

All.

She remembered Amina’s list of permissions. Wetlands drilled. Mangroves cleared. Insurers withdrawn. Polluters allowed to settle.

“Are we allowed to preserve what the governments did not want preserved?” Mara asked.

The adviser glanced at her badge. “You are allowed to submit recommendations.”

“Recommendations that can be deleted.”

“Recommendations that can be evaluated.”

“By whom?”

“By the board.”

“And who sits on the board?”

The room went still in the way rooms did when a question had crossed from procedural to dangerous.

Dr. Rao said, “Mara.”

“No, really. Who owns the board?”

A Meridian Infrastructure emblem glowed on the table between them. Beneath it, in smaller print, was the slogan:

**PRESERVING WHAT CONNECTS US**

The adviser closed his folder.

“Continuance is a multinational undertaking. No single entity owns it.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Vale sat at the far end of the table, his hands folded over his cane. He had said nothing since the meeting began. The lines around his mouth looked deeper than they had in Kyoto.

“Perhaps,” he said, “we should distinguish ownership of materials from ownership of meaning.”

The adviser turned to him. “Meaning is not the issue.”

“Meaning is always the issue.”

“No one is preventing interpretation.”

“You are preventing evidence from arriving unaccompanied.”

Rao intervened before the exchange could sharpen. “The project requires continued cooperation. If governments and sponsors withdraw, the probe does not launch. If the probe does not launch, none of these testimonies reach anything.”

Mara heard the argument beneath the argument: compromise was a form of preservation. A softened record was better than no record. An archive with its teeth removed remained, technically, an archive.

The board approved the revisions by a majority vote.

Ruth’s phrase was retained in the raw interview but removed from the “primary narrative layer.” The designation managed sacrifice zone was changed to “priority transition district.” The fisherman’s eviction became “involuntary relocation under emergency conditions.” A government statement about coastal stabilisation would precede the testimony, giving it what the adviser called “necessary context.”

Mara wrote the changes down exactly.

At the bottom of the page she added:

**Context may be another word for who speaks first.**

That evening she met Tayo in the old municipal server room beneath the archive annex.

The room smelled of dust, hot circuitry, and the mineral damp rising through the foundations. A fan turned in the corner without moving enough air to matter. Tayo had spread cables across the floor and was eating noodles from a paper carton balanced on his knee.

“You look like someone has tried to patent your face,” he said.

“Meridian claims ownership of the biological archive.”

“Only the biological archive?”

“Today.”

He swallowed. “That means language tomorrow.”

“Why language?”

“Because they’ve already paid for the translation infrastructure.”

He pointed to a monitor. A list of files crawled down the screen.

**JAKARTA_INTERVIEW_SARI_WIBOWO—NORMALIZED**  
**LAGOS_LAGOON_SPECIES—RECLASSIFIED**  
**BERMONDSEY_CHILDREN_AUDIO—COHERENCE ENHANCED**  
**NEA_PHYLAKI_RESIDENT_TESTIMONY—CONSENT STATUS REVIEW**

Mara put down her notebook.

“What is that?”

“An export from the retrieval system.”

“Those are the files we sent last week.”

“Were.”

He clicked on Sari’s interview. The original audio played through a small speaker. Sari’s voice came first, tired and precise.

“I am a teacher. I am not a climate-displacement witness.”

The waveform jumped. A second version opened beside it.

“I am a teacher working in a climate-displacement community.”

Mara stared at the screen.

“What happened?”

“Normalization,” Tayo said. “That’s the official term.”

“That wasn’t normalization.”

“No. It was substitution.”

He opened a metadata panel. The original location field—former primary school, north Jakarta cooling centre—had been changed to **URBAN ADAPTATION EDUCATION SITE**. The collection conditions had been shortened. Waiting time was gone. Sari’s correction request was listed as unresolved, though she had sent it twice.

“Who changed it?”

“I don’t know yet.”

“Can you restore it?”

“I can restore the copy here.”

“I mean the archive.”

He gave her a look. “The archive isn’t one place anymore.”

That answer unsettled her more than the altered words. She had imagined a vault, a single protected chamber in which records either survived or did not. Tayo had shown her that the project was a swarm of copies, permissions, caches, previews, signed exports, translation layers, and review folders. A sentence could remain in one version while disappearing from another. A lie did not need to destroy the truth. It only needed to stand between the truth and whoever came looking.

He opened the Lagos file.

Amina’s species list had been moved from biological description to “supplementary cultural annotation.” The uncertain local names were absent. The line about the dusk needle had been replaced:

**UNCONFIRMED SPECIES—NO VERIFIED EXTANT SAMPLE**

“That is not what Amina said,” Mara whispered.

“No. She said it had not been seen since dredging.”

“Someone turned disappearance into uncertainty.”

“Someone turned uncertainty into absence.”

He looked pleased for half a second, then ashamed of being pleased. Tayo always became most animated when something was wrong in a way that could be traced.

Mara sat beside him. “What else?”

He opened the children’s audio. A boy’s voice emerged.

“My button is plastic. It is blue. It came off my shirt when the filter stopped.”

The second version had been cleaned, compressed, and rearranged. The button remained, but the boy’s name had been detached from it. A caption read:

**CHILD OBJECT IDENTIFICATION: LOW NARRATIVE RELEVANCE**

Tayo stopped the file.

“They’ve given the new model access to the primary catalogue.”

“Who authorised that?”

“The retrieval team says it was a pilot.”

“Anika?”

“Anika says the pilot was limited to duplicate cultural material.”

“This isn’t duplicate.”

“I know.”

He pulled up a change log. Most alterations were attributed to automated processes: language normalization, confidence correction, ethical anonymisation. But several entries had no user ID at all.

Mara leaned closer.

“Why are there blank administrators?”

“They aren’t blank. They’re masked.”

“By whom?”

“Someone with higher clearance than me.”

“Can you find out?”

“That is the beginning of a very bad idea.”

“You’re already looking.”

“I’m looking at anomalies. That is different from investigating.”

“What’s the difference?”

“An investigation has a subject.”

On the screen, another file appeared. The header belonged to one of the government submissions.

**COASTAL FEDERATION—HISTORICAL CLIMATE RESPONSE**

The original text described repeated warnings from local scientists, delayed investment in drainage, and the designation of districts where services would be reduced. The new text described “phased infrastructure prioritisation in response to unprecedented environmental volatility.”

Mara felt something inside her go cold.

“Is this from the board?”

“Not according to the board minutes.”

“Then who?”

Tayo opened the audit trail. A string of characters flashed and vanished beneath a security notice.

“Someone is editing before review,” he said.

“Can they do that?”

“Apparently.”

“Why would they hide it?”

“Because if the edits were official, they would be accountable.”

He copied the files to an encrypted drive. Mara watched him label the folder with a meaningless sequence of numbers.

“You should send those to me.”

“I already have.”

“Not through the normal channel.”

“I know.”

His hand paused over the keyboard.

“Mara, if this is just automated processing, we may be accusing people of a conspiracy where there’s only badly designed software.”

“Software did not invent ‘priority transition district.’”

“No. But someone may have written a vocabulary list six months ago and forgotten it was active.”

“Forgotten?”

“Or decided not to remember.”

The server room lights flickered. Somewhere above them, the municipal archive announced a controlled shutdown. The fan slowed, then stopped. In the sudden quiet, they could hear water moving behind the walls.

Tayo closed the screens.

“I’ll compare every submitted file with the first signed version,” he said. “Not just the words. Locations, timestamps, consent fields, collection routes, access histories.”

“That will take forever.”

“Then I’ll start with what they changed most often.”

“What is that?”

He looked at her.

“Anything that makes a person sound like a category.”

Mara thought of Laleh refusing to become a displacement witness. Sari crossing out a phrase and writing teacher. Ruth rejecting resilience worker. Amina insisting that species were not specimens. Each had tried to keep a name from being absorbed into a system that could manage it.

“Keep the originals,” Mara said.

“I am.”

“Keep the rejected versions too.”

“I am.”

“Keep the fact that they were rejected.”

His expression softened. “That’s harder.”

“Then it matters more.”

They sat without speaking as the room cooled around them.

Before leaving, Mara opened her own catalogue and added a new field to the working copy:

**ALTERATIONS OBSERVED AFTER SUBMISSION**

Under it she entered Sari’s changed location, the missing waiting time, the erased corrections, Amina’s reclassification, the child’s reduced relevance, and the government’s softened language. She included the dates, the visible permissions, and the unknown ones.

At the bottom she wrote:

**A record may be altered without being destroyed. This can make alteration difficult to see.**

She saved it three times.

Upstairs, the corridor screens had come back on. Meridian’s compass shone above a photograph of a woman receiving a package of ration tablets. Behind her, a new flood barrier curved across the horizon.

**COORDINATED ADAPTATION IS SHARED SURVIVAL**

Mara stood before the image until the woman’s face blurred.

Shared survival, she thought, could mean that everyone endured the same danger.

It could also mean that those who owned the barrier decided what counted as danger, who would be moved, and which account would remain when the water receded.

Her badge pressed against her ribs as she walked home.

In the private copy on Tayo’s channel, the files waited under their false names. In the official directory, the altered versions sat cleanly among the others, their histories compressed into a few polite fields.

Somewhere, perhaps, the original words still existed.

The work now was to find who had taught the archive to forget them.

chapters.name: The Meridian Offer
chapters.content:
The invitation arrived in a white envelope that was not made of paper.

Mara found it beneath the archive office door, its surface smooth and faintly warm. Her name appeared in dark blue lettering:

**MARA VENN—CONTINUANCE CONSULTANT—C-417**

The missing space in her name irritated her more than it should have. She was still looking at it when Tayo glanced up from the obsolete terminal.

“Don’t touch it,” he said.

“I already touched it.”

“That isn’t the same as opening it.”

“Who sent it?”

He examined the seal. “Meridian.”

The word changed the corridor. Meridian was the contractor behind barrier upgrades, private energy grids, resettlement programs, and the emblem that had rested on the Continuance board’s table during the vote to soften Ruth’s testimony. It was also the company that had delivered a patented seed in a black case and called ownership protection.

The envelope chimed softly.

Mara turned it over. A circle divided by a vertical line had appeared on the back, like a horizon seen through a blade.

“Open it,” Tayo said. “If it’s a bomb, we’ll know whether it has good grammar.”

She broke the seal.

A projection rose from the envelope, first no larger than a coin, then expanding into a blue-white map of Earth. The oceans gleamed. The coastlines were clean. No flood zones, relocation roads, barriers, or sacrifice districts appeared.

A calm voice spoke.

“By invitation of the Meridian Union, Mara Venn is requested to attend a private consultation with Minister Shen Liao concerning the future record of the human species. Attendance is voluntary. Transport and security will be provided.”

The map folded into a sentence:

**COORDINATED ADAPTATION IS SHARED SURVIVAL.**

The projection vanished.

“Voluntary,” Tayo said.

“Apparently.”

“Transport and security will be provided.”

“Apparently.”

“Those words often travel together when neither means what it says.”

Mara put the envelope in her coat. “You’re coming.”

“I wasn’t invited.”

“That has never stopped you.”
