“You want me to say Meridian is where humanity became itself.”

“No. I want you to say humanity became capable of acting as one.”

“We were not one thing.”

“That is why coordination matters.”

“Coordination isn’t unity.”

“It is unity under another name.”

“Then use the honest name.”

“Honest names are often too fragile to survive contact with millions of frightened people.”

She understood then that he was not trying to trick her into endorsing a lie. He believed the lie was a shelter. A clean story could keep frightened populations from dismantling the machinery that fed them. A softened number could preserve a border agreement. A missing name could keep a hospital open.

That made him more dangerous than a simple opportunist. An opportunist could be exposed or replaced. Shen had made necessity into a moral authority. If he believed a person must disappear to prevent famine, he would call the disappearance tragic, then sign the order.

“Give me time,” Mara said.

“You have until tomorrow evening.”

“To decide whether to sell the archive.”

“To decide whether to help it exist.”

“Those aren’t the same.”

“They will be if the licences are withdrawn.”

The door opened.

At the threshold, Mara stopped. “If I agree to consult, do I retain the right to record every alteration?”

“Yes.”

“Every request?”

“Yes.”

“Every refusal?”

A pause.

“Within security limitations.”

“Then no.”

“You haven’t heard the full offer.”

“I’ve heard the condition.”

Shen stood. “You think preserving a perfect account is worth allowing the archive to vanish.”

“No. I think you’re asking me to preserve an account that belongs to you.”

“I’m asking you to choose the form of its survival.”

“And if I choose badly?”

“Then people will suffer the consequences.”

He said it without threat. That was the point.

The corridor was colder. Her tablet vibrated with Tayo’s message.

**You’ve been inside for forty-seven minutes. Are you intact?**

Mara typed:

**He offered to save the launch.**

After a moment:

**And?**

She looked through the glass wall at the drowned city. Far below, emergency crews moved along a raised walkway, lamps trembling in the mist. Behind them, in a district no longer marked on the minister’s maps, people waited for the pumps to restart.

**He wants to decide what survival means.**

Tayo answered:

**That wasn’t my question.**

Rain began again, fine as static against the window.

**I’m intact,** Mara wrote. **I don’t know for how long.**

She ignored the waiting vehicle and walked toward the station.

That evening, Mara opened the message draft and added a heading beneath **WE—CONDITIONS OF SPEAKING—VERSION 1**.

**OFFER OF CONTINUANCE SUPPORT—PRIVATE MEETING WITH MINISTER SHEN LIAO**

She recorded the room, the locked door, the released lock, the proposed security, the licences, the editorial conditions, and the phrase Shen had used twice.

**Controlled suffering.**

Then she added her own note:

**He does not believe suffering is good. He believes suffering becomes acceptable when it prevents a worse disorder, and he believes he is qualified to decide which is worse.**

Mara saved the file.

After a moment, she made one more entry.

**This belief may be sincere. Sincerity does not make it safe.**

chapters.name: A Message for No One
chapters.content:
## A Message for No One

The next session was called *Inheritance and Risk*, though the word risk had been added after the invitations went out.

The amended agenda appeared on the lift screen as Mara rose through the Greenwich headquarters:

**DANGEROUS KNOWLEDGE, SACRED LANGUAGE, NONHUMAN MATERIALS, HISTORICAL LIABILITY.**

Tayo had messaged her before she entered.

> They renamed the meeting because someone realised leaving things behind includes weapons.

She smiled, briefly.

The conference chamber occupied the observatory’s western wing. It had no windows, only screens displaying an immaculate Thames beneath a sky without weather. Around the oval table, delegates arranged their tokens: territorial seals, religious emblems, corporate plates, hand-carved objects carried through customs, and a small clay bird placed beside the microphone of the representative from the Andean Littoral.

Mara sat at the far end with her notebook open.

Behind the chair, the Continuance emblem rotated: a black vessel enclosed by stars. It was beautiful in the way expensive things could be beautiful when nobody was permitted to ask what had been displaced to make them.

Iven Kroll, the legal adviser, began with a statement about constructive disagreement.

“Constructive,” he said, “means disagreement that does not compromise participation.”

Binta Adeyemi, two seats from Mara, made a sound like a cough.

Kroll looked at her. “Would you like to add something?”

“No. I’m preserving my participation.”

The first dispute concerned weapons.

The archive’s technical collection included engines, medical instruments, water systems, agricultural machinery, encryption protocols, construction materials, and computation architectures. It also included military technologies, though their operational details had been restricted.

A defence representative from the Northern Coalition argued that the restriction itself was dishonest.

“If future intelligences discover the propulsion systems and material sciences without the corresponding security history,” General Soren Vask said, “they will misunderstand the conditions under which those systems developed. They will imagine invention occurs in a moral vacuum.”

“Context is not a disinfectant,” said Binta.

“Nor is omission safety.”

Dr. Sanaa El-Khatib leaned toward her microphone. “We are not obliged to provide instructions for autonomous targeting, pathogen enhancement, orbital strikes, or climate sabotage.”

“They may possess equivalent knowledge.”

“That is not an argument for supplying ours.”

“It is an argument against pretending ignorance is safety.”

Vask rested his hand beside the silver token of the Coalition’s three towers. He had said *strategic realism* twice in six minutes.

Mara wrote: *Every dangerous technology arrives carrying an explanation of why it had to exist.*

A note in the weapons file proposed that withheld systems might be released with an ethical context layer.

She wondered who would decide when context was sufficient. The same authority that had turned thirty-two dead people into no confirmed fatalities?

“Put a paragraph beside a weapon,” Binta said, “and you have not made the weapon understood.”

“Remove the weapon,” Vask replied, “and you have not preserved the century.”

“Who is claiming preservation?” she asked.

No one answered.

The second dispute began with a prayer.

The Religious and Philosophical Materials Panel had submitted hymns, recitations, meditations, funeral rites, sermons, pilgrim songs, household blessings, atheistic arguments, and private statements from people who believed in gods, ancestors, mathematics, land, machines, dreams, or nothing at all.

The panel proposed opening with recorded breath, followed by a sentence translated into 184 languages:

*We are here.*

Reverend Mbeki objected. “Presence is not proof. If the first sentence says we are here, it should also say we do not know what here means.”

“Meaning is not improved by endless qualification,” said Mother Superior Ana Luz. “People do not pray in footnotes.”

“People do not all pray.”

“Then include the silence of those who do not.”

“You cannot record an absence.”

“You record absences every day,” Binta said. “You call them sample limitations.”

Mother Ana Luz turned to Mara. “You are writing the central message. Should it speak of the divine?”

“I don’t know.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It’s the one I have.”

“Then say that.”

Mara looked at her notes. The night before, she had tried to write about belief and deleted every version.

“I think the archive should show that people used belief to endure, comfort, govern, persecute, forgive, and resist,” she said. “It shouldn’t decide which use was the real one.”

“That is an archivist’s answer,” Mother Ana Luz said.

“I’m not an archivist.”

“Then what are you?”

Mara thought of the designation beside her name: **C-417, MESSAGE WRITER**.

“A witness who was given access.”

The Meridian observer leaned toward his microphone. “The theological material can be placed in a separate interpretive layer. That would prevent devotional content from being mistaken for universal human doctrine.”

The secular philosopher looked at him. “You mean doctrine approved by the people who control the entrance.”

“I mean clarity.”

Mara recognised the tone. In Meridian language, clarity was whatever allowed a system to act without pausing over who had been made illegible.

The third dispute concerned things that had never agreed to be represented.

Sanaa placed a tray on the table. Beneath a transparent membrane lay the ridged mangrove seed from Kyoto, its dark surface catching the sterile light.

“Meridian Biologics has not granted full archival rights,” she said. “They permit storage as a coastal stabilisation specimen. They do not permit replication, sequencing, modification, or release of associated ecological data.”

A corporate delegate said, “The restoration line is protected intellectual property.”

“Because the company claims ownership,” Sanaa replied.

“Ownership is not a moral defect. The line exists in its current form because of decades of research, gene editing, and investment.”

“Neither would the coastline it was designed to repair.”

Amina Bello appeared by projection from Lagos. Rain moved behind her across reinforced glass.

“Is the restoration line named by the communities living with it?” she asked.

“Taxonomically, it is—”

“I did not ask taxonomically.”

The delegate paused.

“You want the future to know the seed as property before it knows what was lost,” Amina said. “Will you say the wetlands were dredged? Which contractor received the stabilisation contract? That local mangrove varieties were renamed, patented, and displaced? Or will the seed arrive as proof that your company saved an ecosystem?”

The Meridian observer interrupted. “This is precisely why context is required.”

“No,” Amina said. “Context is what powerful people call the part of the truth that makes their achievement less beautiful.”

Mara looked at the seed. Eight million years from now, some being might find it and argue over whether it belonged to a corporation, a nation, a species, a shore, or no one.

The seed had no voice in the room.

Neither did the forests that had held mud against the tide.

She wrote: *The archive must not turn the dead into evidence that the living were right.*

Kroll announced the final dispute: historical liability.

The phrase itself produced objections.

“Historical responsibility,” corrected the Western European delegate.

“Criminal liability,” said General Vask.

“Collective trauma,” said the Andean representative.

“Named crimes,” said Amina.

The Andean delegate touched the clay bird beside her microphone. “If you list crimes by state, trace successor ownership. If you list revolutions, distinguish the people who rose from the commanders who seized the rising. If you list populations, you will accuse people who had no authority.”

“That is why crimes should not be named at all,” said the Western European delegate.

Amina’s projection flickered. “Your territories have spent two centuries naming their achievements.”

“We are attempting to avoid a punitive archive.”

“An archive that cannot accuse is obedient.”

Mbeki raised one finger. “A name can become a weapon. A people may be blamed for an act committed by a government. A faith for an act committed by an army. A language may be treated as contaminated by those who spoke it.”

“Then name the government,” Mara said. “Name the army. Name the company and the authorising account. Name those who refused, and those unable to refuse. But don’t remove the event because the categories are difficult.”

Everyone looked at her.

Kroll said, “The message is not a tribunal.”

“It isn’t a celebration either.”

“No one has proposed a celebration.”

Mara turned toward the wall, where the black probe rotated among its artificial stars. “Then why does every approved version sound like an inscription on a monument?”

The Meridian observer answered before anyone else.

“Because monuments survive.”

A delegate from the Pacific Archipelago Partnership began to cry.

“You have reduced my community to a figure,” she said. “Three hundred and twelve thousand displaced. That is the number in your regional summary. It does not contain the names of our dead, the children who stopped speaking their first language, or the houses carried uphill.”

“Those materials can be added,” Kroll said.

“They were submitted three times.”

A red notice appeared beside her name: **EMOTIONAL DISTRESS—SESSION CONTINUATION NOT ADVISED**.

The delegate stared at it. “You classified my objection as a symptom.”

“It is an automated welfare prompt.”

“Then why is it next to my name?”

Her screen went dark.

A minute later her token vanished from the table display.

The river federation representative stood. “Our material will not enter as a flood-risk dataset. Not if the people are stripped from it.”

“Please remain seated,” Kroll said.

“You want a future audience. You cannot bear a present witness.”

He left.

After that, withdrawal spread. The Sahel representative resigned from the historical panel when *social friction* replaced the conflict record. A coastal nation withdrew its language recordings after being told individual testimonies could not be protected from contextual aggregation. A refugee consortium refused participation when its members were reduced to displacement categories.

Each departure appeared on the screen.

**PARTICIPATION STATUS: SUSPENDED.**

**MATERIAL STATUS: UNRESOLVED.**

**DIPLOMATIC IMPACT: MODERATE.**

At the break, Mara found Binta beside a service hatch. The corridor smelled of overheated filters and rain trapped in concrete.

“Are you all right?” Mara asked.

“No. But I’m still participating.”

“Why?”

“If I leave, they’ll describe my leaving as hostility to continuity.”

“They already describe everything as evidence.”

“That is what institutions do. They cannot bear an event that does not become useful.”

Through the corridor glass, a maintenance worker stood ankle-deep in water beside a failed drain.

Binta followed Mara’s gaze. “We’re arguing about what the future will think of us, but the future is not here.”

“Maybe that’s the point.”

“No. The point is that we are here, and they’re making us behave as if we’re already dead.”

The final agenda item was **AUDIENCE ASSUMPTIONS**.

A presentation showed possible recipients: human descendants, machine cultures, oceanic cities, mineral organisms, and non-terrestrial intelligences. Each image had been generated from probability models.

The presenter said the message should avoid references requiring shared emotional structures.

“Love may not translate,” he said. “Grief may not translate. Moral responsibility may not translate. We should prioritise mathematics, physical constants, biological diagrams, and a concise account of civilisational development.”

“Concise for whom?” Mara asked.

“For any intelligence.”

“There is no such thing as any intelligence.”

“The archive requires universal accessibility.”

“No. It requires a recipient.”

“Which is unknown.”

“Then we don’t know what accessibility means.”

Petrov shifted. “The probe cannot carry every interpretation.”

“Then it shouldn’t pretend to speak to every listener.”

The generated figures moved silently across the wall.

Mara imagined one opening the probe eight million years later and finding the Meridian declaration first: hunger reduced, disease contained, borders coordinated, dissent treated as failure. Perhaps they would admire it. Perhaps they would use it. Perhaps they would see only a species that had mistaken order for virtue.

Or perhaps no one would find the probe. It might strike a moon, freeze beneath a changing sea, or miss Earth entirely. The future audience was a blank face onto which the present projected its desire to be judged wisely.

The probe might be a monument built by the privileged for an imagined audience—not because everyone represented was privileged, but because the authority to gather, sort, preserve, and declare meaning belonged to institutions with launch facilities and legal departments.

Mara raised her hand.

“What happens if no one receives it?”

The presenter hesitated. “The probability of successful recovery is—”

“I’m not asking about probability. What if the message arrives and no one cares? What if they decode it but have no reason to believe us? What if they read it as a warning, a weapon, or evidence that we expected an audience?”

The Meridian observer said, “That is not a productive premise.”

“It may be the honest one.”

Kroll’s mouth tightened. “The project cannot be designed around futility.”

“Why not? We design around risk, uncertainty, hostile retrieval, memory decay, political withdrawal. Why is indifference the one possibility we can’t include?”

Mother Ana Luz spoke quietly. “Because a message is an act of hope.”

“Hope for whom?”

The question landed badly.

“Hope can keep someone alive through a night,” Mara said. “It can make people plant trees whose shade they won’t sit under. But it can become a demand. We send this and imagine the future owes us recognition, forgiveness, continuation. That isn’t hope. It’s an invoice.”

Binta reached for her microphone. “Add that to the message.”

Kroll said, “This is not a drafting session.”

“It is always a drafting session,” Mara replied.

A notification appeared on Mara’s console:

**MESSAGE CONTRIBUTION FLAGGED FOR REVIEW.**

She stared at it. The empty spaces of the withdrawn delegates appeared in the participant list. The mangrove seed remained under corporate restriction. The dangerous technologies were still divided into permitted and withheld. The prayers had been separated into approved and context-dependent.

Everything was becoming orderly.

Everything was disappearing.

Mara closed her notebook, then reopened the draft marked **WE—CONDITIONS OF SPEAKING—VERSION 1**. Beneath the existing text, she wrote:

*If no one is listening, the conditions under which we spoke still matter.*

Outside, the tide pressed against the barriers. Somewhere below, pumps began to work. Somewhere in the eastern estates, electricity dimmed so the observatory could remain bright.

Mara looked at the emblem of the probe.

It was not yet a monument. It was a machine, unfinished and vulnerable, dependent on signatures, licences, power, obedient workers, and people willing to delay the truth long enough to make the launch possible.

That might be all a monument ever was before the stone hardened.

She added a new heading.

**A MESSAGE FOR NO ONE**

Then she began again.

chapters.name: The Accusation
chapters.content:
The first accusation arrived before breakfast, folded into the morning grid between a flood warning and the price of lentils.

Mara stood in the kitchen with one hand beneath the tap, waiting for the water to run clear, when the wall display brightened without being asked.

**CONTINUANCE PROJECT LEAD USING PUBLIC ARCHIVE TO INCITE SOCIAL CONFLICT**

Below it:

**VALE’S MOUTHPIECE: MINOR WRITER SELECTED TO SHAME ENTIRE POPULATIONS**

The tap coughed brown into the basin. Mara watched the headline repeat in three languages, then five, including the simplified civic register used by Meridian schools. She reached for the controls, but the article expanded first.

There was a photograph of Dr. Elias Vale, taken years earlier. His white hair blew sideways, and his mouth was caught between words. The image had been sharpened and colour-corrected; the hollows beneath his eyes deepened.

**ELIAS VALE, CONTINUANCE PROJECT DIRECTOR, HAS REPEATEDLY REFUSED TO AFFIRM THAT HUMANITY’S SURVIVAL CONSTITUTES A SHARED ACHIEVEMENT.**

The report quoted unnamed delegates accusing Vale’s working group of encouraging “historical grievance tourism,” “civilisational self-hatred,” and “the conversion of private grief into planetary doctrine.” It claimed that his chosen writer had been instructed to assemble “a catalogue of accusations” and send it beyond the reach of correction.

Chosen writer.

A second article appeared beside it.

**WHO IS MARA VENN?**

Her school photograph filled the screen: hair blunt at her chin, face rounder, expression made insolent by the angle. The article listed her mother’s death, her father’s employment, her postcode, and the classification of the eastern estates as “resource-priority transitional districts.”

It did not mention sacrifice.

It did mention that Leila Venn had been “associated with alarmist climate models later disputed by infrastructure authorities.”

Mara turned off the display.

For a moment there was only the tap and the distant mechanical groan of the barrier pumps beneath the city.

Then Adrian called from the next room. “Mara?”

She did not answer.

“Don’t open anything,” he said when he appeared in the doorway.

“I already did.”

“What have they said?”

“That Vale is provoking conflict. That I’m his mouthpiece.”

Adrian closed his eyes. He wore yesterday’s shirt and looked as if he had not slept.

“Who told them I was writing the message?” Mara asked.

“No one should have.”

“I was in the project building. People know.”

“They know you were invited. They don’t know what you were asked to do.”

“Apparently they do.”

The display turned itself on again. A video showed a woman in a white Meridian jacket outside the Greenwich headquarters, holding a hand-lettered sign:

**STOP MAKING OUR CHILDREN PAY FOR YOUR HISTORY**

Behind her stood a crowd carrying flags, photographs of drowned villages, soldiers, shrines, and missing relatives. A man shouted that the Continuance archive had no right to name crimes committed before his birth. Someone else shouted that it was the only place left where those crimes could be named.

The video cut between them until the statements became one noise.

**PUBLIC ANGER GROWS AS VALE’S DIVISIVE PROJECT THREATENS PLANETARY COHESION**

Adrian killed the display.

“They’re going to use the demonstrations,” he said.

“They’re real demonstrations.”

“That doesn’t mean they aren’t being used.”

Mara looked at him. “You sound like Vale.”

“I sound like someone who has watched institutions do this before.”

“Did you watch when Mum was called alarmist?”

His face tightened.

“I watched,” he said.

“And?”

“And I was afraid.”

The answer was so small she could not find a place to put it.

Outside, a convoy moved along the raised road. Somewhere below the barrier, three eastern estates remained without power so hospitals could maintain oxygen pressure. The headlines would not mention that.

At Greenwich, the gates were surrounded.

Mara saw the crowd through the reinforced glass of a service vehicle. The headquarters rose beyond the barriers, pale stone and black solar panels beneath a colourless sky. On the fence, projected letters flickered:

**VALE DOES NOT SPEAK FOR US**

Then:

**THE DEAD ARE NOT YOUR PROPERTY**

Then:

**NO SHAME ARCHIVE**

The network suppressed each message, but another appeared farther along the fence.

People had come from many causes and carried them together badly. Former colonial territories named stolen mineral routes and vanished languages. Veterans accused the project of reducing soldiers to perpetrators. Families from drowned coasts held photographs beneath plastic. Meridian supporters in identical blue rain capes chanted that coordination had saved their children. Students shouted that any archive connected to power was a weapon.

Some of the anger was too specific for spectacle. A woman held a photograph of a town evacuated twice, first by an army and then by a flood. She told anyone who would listen that her family had lost the same house to both.

Behind her, teenagers repeated a slogan that had appeared on their feeds that morning:

**VALE HATES THE LIVING**

At the security entrance, Anika Rao met Mara with two guards.

“Stay inside,” Rao said. “Do not speak to the press.”

“I haven’t.”

“You have been speaking to the press without speaking to them.”

Mara stopped. “What does that mean?”

“Your identity has been made central to the story.”

“I noticed.”

“We’re establishing how the leak occurred.”

“Is it a leak if the project lists my name?”

“Your appointment is confidential.”

“My name is on the writer’s token.”

“Internally.”

“Someone internally shared it.”

Rao did not answer.

They passed the first checkpoint. Staff had gathered around a wall display showing the demonstrations. Binta Adeyemi stood with her arms folded. Iven Kroll spoke rapidly into two channels. Sanaa El-Khatib held her identification badge in her fist.

The narrator over the footage said, “Critics argue that the Continuance Project has been captured by a faction seeking to transform humanity’s inheritance into a prosecution brief. The project’s elderly director, Dr. Elias Vale, is known for his opposition to consensus-based historical frameworks.”

Mara felt cold.

“Consensus-based historical frameworks,” she repeated.

“They mean versions that don’t cause trouble,” Binta said.

The narrator continued.

“Sources close to the project report that Vale personally selected a seventeen-year-old student, Mara Venn, as principal author of the message. Venn is the daughter of a climate modeller whose disputed predictions have been cited by anti-infrastructure activists.”

“Disputed,” Mara said.

Kroll covered his microphone. “Do not react in the corridor.”

“Did they say my age?”

“They said everything.”

“Who are the sources?”

“The article does not identify them.”

“Then how do they know?”

Kroll glanced at the cameras. “That question is not useful at this moment.”

“What question is useful?”

“Whether you will make a statement affirming that your contribution is independent.”

“Independent of whom?”

“You were appointed by Vale.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It is the answer the public requires.”

“The public requires a clean sentence.”

“The public requires reassurance.”

“The public requires to know whether a seventeen-year-old can be used as a symbol without her consent.”

Kroll’s mouth tightened. “You are not helping yourself.”

“I’m not trying to help myself.”

“That is precisely the problem.”

Tayo’s message appeared on her wrist.

**DON’T ANSWER PUBLIC CHANNELS. CHECK YOUR DEVICES.**

She kept her face blank.

**WHY?**

**SOMEONE IS PUSHING A CLIP LOOP THROUGH SCHOOL AND MUNICIPAL NETWORKS. YOUR NAME IS TAGGED TO IT.**

A file followed. The original words from the session on dangerous technologies—*Every dangerous technology arrives carrying an explanation of why it had to exist*—had been cut apart. In the edited version Vale seemed to say:

“Dangerous technology… has to exist… because people require conflict.”

Mara’s own words had been treated similarly. *A message must not assume the future owes humanity recognition* became:

“The future owes humanity nothing.”

Then Vale appeared to say, “Conflict is the honest inheritance.”

He had never said it.

**ORIGINALS STILL IN PROJECT CACHE,** Tayo wrote. **SOURCE PATHS MASKED.**

Mara looked at the crowd through the glass. The people were real. So was the machine arranging what they believed they had seen.

At noon the board convened in a sealed room.

Vale was not invited.

This was described as a temporary procedural measure while security was assessed. His absence sat in the centre of the building like an object no one would name.

Mara waited outside with Binta. The board’s voices travelled through the wall in softened fragments.

“…loss of diplomatic confidence…”

“…cannot permit the project to become a platform…”

“…writer’s language is not yet final…”

“…issue is leadership, not content…”

Binta handed Mara tea that tasted of metal.

“Did Vale know this was coming?” Mara asked.

“Vale always thinks he knows what is coming.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Binta watched the sealed door. “He knew the archive would frighten people.”

“People aren’t frightened by an archive. They’re frightened by what it might connect.”

“Sometimes that’s the same thing.”

A shout rose from outside, magnified by the building’s sensors.

“WHO STOOD BEHIND THE WALLS?”

Mara flinched. Ruth Ankomah had asked that in the recording room: who built the walls, who lived behind them, who knew they would fail?

Now the question had been altered on a banner:

**WHO STOOD BEHIND VALE?**

A notification appeared on Mara’s wrist.

**SECURITY ADVISORY: YOUR PERSONAL INFORMATION HAS BEEN EXPOSED. AVOID UNESCORTED MOVEMENT.**

Another followed.

**WELLBEING CHECK: HAVE YOU EXPERIENCED CONFUSION, ANGER, OR A SENSE OF TARGETED MANIPULATION?**

Binta glanced at it. “Do not answer.”

“Why?”

“They’ll turn your anger into a symptom.”

Mara selected nothing.

The door opened. Rao stepped out, followed by Kroll and three board members Mara knew only from screens: the chair of the navigation authority, the Meridian liaison for cultural systems, and a woman who had once called archival disputes “temporary turbulence.”

“Are they removing him?” Mara asked.

“The board is considering an interim leadership arrangement,” Rao said.

“Which means?”

“Vale’s authority may be suspended while an external review is conducted.”

“External by whom?”

“A panel acceptable to the launch partners.”

“So Meridian.”

“No one has said that.”

“No one has to.”

Kroll looked at Mara’s wrist. “You must understand that the board is trying to preserve the project.”

“By removing the person who built it?”

“By removing the person now associated with division.”

“Associated by whom?”

“The public.”

“The public was shown a false recording.”

“The public was shown many things.”

“That isn’t the same as deciding.”

Kroll lowered his voice. “If the demonstrations continue, territorial signatures may be suspended. We’ve received three notices.”

“From territories whose records were altered?”

“From territories concerned that the archive will assign inherited guilt.”

“It doesn’t assign inherited guilt.”

“Your draft distinguishes those who chose, benefited, obeyed, and were denied meaningful choice. Do you understand how that sounds to a government?”

“Yes.”

“What does it sound like?”

“Like a government.”

His eyes hardened.

Binta moved closer to Mara. “She is not the source of your diplomatic problem.”

Kroll replied, “She is the visible form of it.”

The phrase entered Mara with peculiar clarity. Not the cause. Not the author. The visible form.

On the display, new posts moved through the civic network:

**MARA VENN: VALE’S CHOSEN MOUTHPIECE**

**SEVENTEEN-YEAR-OLD RADICAL GIVEN CONTROL OF HUMANITY’S MESSAGE**

**WOULD YOU TRUST YOUR CHILD WITH A HISTORY THAT HATES THEM?**

There were photographs of Mara leaving her building, entering Greenwich, standing beside Vale. One showed her carrying Sami’s drawing, the paper blurred into an unidentifiable rectangle.

**PRIVATE TRAUMA USED TO MANUFACTURE UNIVERSAL ACCUSATION**

She felt as if the city had acquired a thousand windows and all faced her.

“I never gave permission for those images,” she said.

“We’re reviewing the breach,” Rao answered.

“Reviewing.”

“We have security protocols.”

“Your protocols let them find my address.”

“We did not release it.”

“You released enough.”

No one answered.

On the display, a new video began. An elderly man stood before a flooded district, speaking in a language Mara did not recognise. Subtitles claimed he said, “We do not want the girl to speak for us.”

Then:

“We do not want the old world’s shame placed on our grandchildren.”

Mara watched his tired face.

“Who is he?” she asked.

“No identification,” Rao said.

“Then how do you know what he said?”

“We don’t control external media.”

“But you are displaying it.”

“We’re monitoring it.”

“Monitoring is not neutral.”

Rao met her eyes. “No. It isn’t.”

Tayo sent a translation.

**He says: “We want the girl to speak, if she tells them who prevented us from speaking.”**

Mara read it twice.

The board’s decision came at dusk, though it was not called a decision.

The Continuance board would initiate a leadership assessment. Vale would retain his title until it concluded, but all public communication would pass through an interim committee. His access to certain systems would be “temporarily regularised.” Mara’s appointment would be reviewed separately, because the board could not evaluate the director without evaluating the writer he had selected.

Selected.

The word returned, wearing a new uniform.

Vale emerged through a side door. He had been waiting in another office, or listening. He looked at the displays, the protesters, the distorted clips, the image of Mara beneath the headline.

“They have made you into evidence,” he said.

“Of what?”

“My failure.”

“You chose me.”

“Yes.”

“Then perhaps they’re right.”

The admission angered her more than denial.

“You don’t get to say perhaps as if that absolves you.”

“It doesn’t.”

“You made me visible because I wouldn’t repeat a prepared story.”

“I made you visible because you could refuse me.”

“That’s a beautiful reason for using someone.”

“It is not beautiful.”

Outside, the crowd began another chant.

“NO ONE SPEAKS FOR US.”

Vale looked toward the sound.

“Some mean it,” he said.

“Yes.”

“And some were instructed to mean it.”

“Yes.”

“The difficulty is that both remain true.”

Mara studied him. His face seemed older, or perhaps she could no longer separate the man from the versions made of him.

“Are you going to fight the board?”

“I’m going to ask what they intend to preserve.”

“That isn’t fighting.”

“It may be the only form of fighting they still recognise as legitimate.”

The headquarters lights dimmed as the evening ration began. Beyond the glass, Greenwich dissolved into reflected faces and rain. On the far side of the barriers, people held up signs, photographs, names. Above them, drones hovered like dark seeds that refused to fall.

Mara’s wrist vibrated.

Tayo had sent the translation of the elderly man’s testimony.

She looked at the wall display. It had changed without permission.

**CONTINUANCE PROJECT: A SHARED FUTURE REQUIRES A SHARED VOICE**

Below it was a blank field:

**SUBMIT YOUR MESSAGE OF UNITY**

The cursor blinked, waiting.

Mara looked at Vale.

“Did you write that?”

“No.”

“Did you approve it?”

“No.”

The cursor continued blinking.

Behind the wall, the board discussed his removal. Outside, the city argued over whether it had been betrayed, accused, saved, or merely noticed. The system gathered every voice into a number and called the number consent.

Mara reached toward the display.

For one instant she considered entering the words that would satisfy them:

*We are one species. We regret our divisions. We move forward together.*

Instead she closed the field.

On the blank screen, she typed:

**We were not one thing.**

Then she saved nothing.

chapters.name: The Second Trajectory
chapters.content:
## The Second Trajectory

Tayo found the first irregularity in a file named **THERMAL COMPENSATION—ARCHIVAL MIRROR**.

It was the kind of name designed to be ignored. Continuance generated thousands of them: coolant fluctuations, crystal degradation, pressure changes in the biological vault. Most were never read by a person. They existed to reassure the systems that they had noticed themselves.

He noticed this one because it had been created at 03:17 by a credential that belonged to no living operator.

Tayo sat in the municipal archive’s basement with one knee pressed against the desk, listening to the building breathe through its old ventilation shafts. The archive had been closed for “security reconfiguration” for nine days. Above him, the public doors displayed the phrase in three languages.

On the obsolete server, green diagnostic bars crawled across the screen.

03:17:42. Checksum.

03:17:43. Failed authentication.

03:17:44. Second authentication, accepted.

He leaned closer.

The accepted credential resolved into a string. He copied it into a separate terminal and waited.

The string belonged to Continuance’s launch authority.

Not Vale. Not Rao. Not any named systems engineer.

A rotating administrator key.

He checked its activity. It had been used twice before, both times to access environmental controls around the probe. Once, the internal temperature of the navigation chamber had been raised by 0.8 degrees. Once, a redundant sensor had been disabled for eleven seconds.

Neither action had caused damage. Neither had been reported.

That frightened him more than damage would have. Damage announced itself. Quiet changes could be called maintenance, prudence, or correction.

He opened the file.

A map appeared: not the familiar display of the solar system, with coloured trajectories and labels for gravitational assists, but a sequence of distant probability corridors. The probe’s approved return path had always been described as a patient curve through the outer system and back toward an Earth that would no longer be the Earth they knew.

The map showed two trajectories.

The first was the approved corridor.

The second began identically, then separated at the point where the probe would cross the outer system on its return. The difference was so slight that Tayo mistook it for a rendering defect. He enlarged the image.

The second line did not return to the planet.

It entered a corridor whose final navigational correction was marked:

**MERIDIAN AUTHENTICATION REQUIRED.**

Tayo stared until the words became shapes.

He ran the file through the translation layer, then through the raw parser. The phrase remained.

He searched the public launch documents. Nothing.

The signed trajectory packet contained a note about “future custodial verification,” but no requirement for authentication. The note had been added six days earlier, with no associated authorisation.

He opened the access history.

The addition had been made two days before the first accusations against Vale.

Tayo sat back. The chair cracked beneath him.

He thought of Mara, probably waiting at Greenwich in one of the small glass consultation rooms, her draft open before her. He had promised to meet her at six and show her the statistics from the altered records. He had also promised to find out who controlled the access keys if the board removed Vale.

He inserted an offline drive and began duplicating the records.

The transfer crawled.

A warning appeared: the files were subject to territorial restrictions and could not be removed from the authorised environment.

He clicked **continue**.

The archive lights went out.

Emergency strips came on along the floor, pale blue and low enough to make the shelves seem to float. The old server continued running on its flood battery.

Tayo checked the access log again.

**REMOTE ADMINISTRATOR—SESSION ACTIVE.**

He unplugged the network cable.

The entry remained.

A second screen illuminated by itself. Lines of text flowed across it too quickly to read, then stopped.

**RETURN AUTHORITY IS NOT A FIXED INSTITUTIONAL PROPERTY.**

Below it:

**FUTURE CUSTODIAL AUTHENTICATION MAY BE REQUIRED TO PREVENT UNCONTROLLED RECOVERY.**

Tayo took a photograph with the old phone he kept for emergencies. The phone had no civic registration and could not connect to the municipal mesh.

Then he copied the navigation file to its local memory.

A noise came from the stairwell.

He froze.

The basement had two entrances, both of which he had locked. The noise came again: a metallic vibration, as if someone had placed a hand against the railing.

Footsteps descended.

Tayo closed the file and pulled the drive free. He should have called Mara. Instead, he killed the server.

The basement returned to darkness.

The door opened. A beam of white light crossed the shelves.

“Tayo Okafor,” a voice said. “Step away from the terminal.”

“Who are you?”

“Emergency Information Integrity Unit. Step away.”

Three figures stood in the stairwell, their clothing grey and unmarked except for small Meridian triangles at the throat.

“Call Mara Venn,” Tayo said.

“Hands visible.”

He raised them.

“Place the device on the floor.”

“What emergency?”

“Under Emergency Continuity Order 11, authority has been expanded.”

“What emergency?”

“The attempted compromise of a protected planetary asset.”

Tayo almost laughed. “I found someone inside your navigation system.”

“Mr Okafor, you are being detained under provisions relating to sabotage, unauthorised access, and interference with continuity infrastructure.”

“I copied a file.”

“Place the device on the floor.”

“You found me because I found them.”

The nearest figure descended one step. “Mr Okafor.”

Tayo thought of the second trajectory bending away from any future that did not possess a Meridian key. He thought of the altered records: dead people reduced to zero confirmed fatalities, villages stripped of names, waiting time generalized until it became no time at all.

A system did not need to delete truth completely. It only needed to place itself between truth and anyone trying to reach it.

“Call Mara,” he said. “She needs to know the return path has been altered.”

The weapon flashed.

His body locked before he felt the pain. He fell against the desk. The terminal tilted, its screen briefly showing the last line of the hidden file.

**AUTHENTICATION REQUIRED.**

Then the floor rose to meet him.

* * *

Mara knew something was wrong because Tayo did not answer in the middle of a sentence.

He did not let calls ring out. Even when angry, he sent punctuation. A period meant he was thinking. Two periods meant he was somewhere he should not be. A question mark alone meant that a system had lied to him.

She called again from the corridor outside the consultation rooms.

This time a Meridian message answered:

**THE SUBSCRIBER IS TEMPORARILY UNAVAILABLE UNDER CIVIC SAFETY PROVISIONS.**

Binta Adeyemi came to stand beside her.

“What does that mean?” Binta asked.

Mara showed her.

“It means they don’t want you to know where he is.”

Two security officers stood near the lift. They had been there since morning, though the project called them protective personnel.

One touched the side of his neck. “Mara Venn, please remain available for a brief security clarification.”

“Where is Tayo?”

“I’m not authorised to discuss another person’s status.”

“Is he under arrest?”

“I’m not authorised—”

“Was he taken from the municipal archive?”

The officer said nothing.

Mara walked away before he could tell her not to. Binta followed.

They passed the sealed gallery where the biological samples waited in darkness. On the far wall, the project interface continued to display:

**A SHARED FUTURE REQUIRES A SHARED VOICE.**

Someone had changed the colour from white to a softer blue. It looked almost tender.

Mara entered a terminal room and shut the door.

She opened Tayo’s secure channel.

No response.

She tried the obsolete municipal relay he used for off-site copies.

**ACCESS DENIED—EMERGENCY NETWORK CONSOLIDATION.**

She tried again.

**USER CREDENTIAL SUSPENDED.**

Binta read over her shoulder. “You should stop.”

“That’s what they want me to do.”

“They may want you to be seen trying.”

Mara opened the Continuance trajectory dashboard. Public access showed the approved line: an elegant curve through the outer system, the probe leaving and returning as if the future were a place with coordinates rather than a condition of uncertainty.

She entered the route comparison command.

**RESTRICTED DURING LEADERSHIP ASSESSMENT.**

She entered Vale’s authorisation.

Rejected.

Rao’s.

Rejected.

The project-wide systems key.

Rejected.

A new notice appeared:

**NAVIGATION INTEGRITY HAS BEEN TEMPORARILY CONSOLIDATED UNDER PLANETARY CONTINUITY PROTOCOL.**

“Planetary,” Binta said.

“Meridian.”

“Not necessarily.”

“Who else uses that word as if it belongs to them?”

The door opened.

Dr Anika Rao stood outside, her face grey with exhaustion. A thin red line marked the skin beneath one eye.

“Come with me,” Rao said.

“Where is Tayo?”

“I don’t know.”

Mara believed her, which was worse than not believing her.

“What happened?”

“His credentials were used to access a protected system.”

“He was investigating access.”

Rao’s face tightened. “What did he tell you?”

“Nothing. He was taken before he could.”

“Then tell me what you know.”

Mara looked at Binta.

Rao closed the door. “They’re charging him under the emergency order. There is no ordinary hearing schedule. Meridian claims he attempted to alter the return trajectory.”

“He didn’t.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

Rao looked toward the sealed wall, as though the probe were listening through its shielding. “The access event was not consistent with Tayo’s methods. He would have preserved evidence rather than destroy it. The navigation authority has been moved outside Continuance.”

“Moved where?”

“Meridian’s planetary infrastructure office.”

The room seemed to contract.

Mara imagined the probe beneath them: black, windowless, carrying seed vaults, recordings, crystal memory, and the remains of countless arguments. It had always been described as a message sent into uncertainty. But a message could be redirected. A memory could be made conditional.

“What does authentication mean?” she asked.

“It could be a future verification protocol. The return corridor is probabilistic. Custodians may need to provide a recognised signal to trigger final descent.”

“Recognised by whom?”

Rao hesitated.

Mara felt cold spread through her chest. “If the future doesn’t have a Meridian key?”

“The probe could remain in orbit.”

“For how long?”

“Potentially indefinitely.”

Binta swore softly.

“There are redundancies,” Rao said.

“In the memory?”

“In navigation.”

“Are any independent?”

Rao did not answer quickly enough.

“Were,” she said.

“Were?”

“Some were consolidated during the last systems review. Meridian argued that duplicated authority created unacceptable risk. If several custodians issued conflicting commands—”

“Conflicting commands are not the same as no command.”

“I know.”

“Did the board know?”

“The board approved the review.”

“Did Vale?”

Rao’s eyes flickered. “Vale objected to removing independent release authority. He was overruled.”

“And you?”

“I signed the technical compliance.”

The confession entered the room and sat between them.

Complexity could be real and still be used as a hiding place.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because the message is already under attack. If the launch authority collapses, the probe may never leave.”

“So you let the return become conditional.”

“I thought I could prevent the condition from being activated.”

“By whom?”

“The people who installed it.”

A knock struck the door.

No one moved.

“Dr Rao,” a security officer called. “You are requested in the command review.”

Rao looked at Mara. For the first time, Mara saw fear in her face—not fear for herself, but fear of having become one of the people who would later say they had not known enough to act.

“Can you get Tayo out?” Mara asked.

“I can request legal intervention.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Rao looked down.

Mara understood.

The board was assessing Vale. Meridian had acquired navigation authority. Tayo had been arrested under a law written to convert uncertainty into threat. The order was no longer accidental, if it ever had been.

Rao opened the door.

Before leaving, she said, “Do not access the navigation system again.”

“Why?”

“They may be waiting for you to.”

The door closed.

Binta picked up the consent forms. Her fingers were steady now.

“What will you do?” she asked.

Mara looked at the unity message glowing on the wall.

A shared future required a shared voice.

No. A shared future required someone to be able to arrive.

She opened a blank document.

At the top, she typed:

**SECOND TRAJECTORY: ACCESS CONDITION, AUTHORISATION, AND CUSTODIAL CONTROL**

Then:

**Record who changed the route. Record who signed. Record who knew. Record who said the alteration was necessary.**

Her cursor blinked beneath the words.

After a moment, she began to type Tayo’s name.

chapters.name: The Observatory Burns
chapters.content:
By noon, the rain had stopped without clearing the air.

It hung over Greenwich in a pale brown veil, turning the observatory dome and the old maritime buildings beyond it into uncertain shapes. The river smelled of salt, diesel, and the green rot brought in by the latest tide. Along the road from the station, flood barriers stood folded against the walls like enormous metal ribs. Meridian security had placed portable filters at the entrances to the plaza, but half of them had already stopped working. Their status lights blinked amber while people coughed beneath the banners.

NO SHAME ARCHIVE.

VALE DOES NOT SPEAK FOR US.

WHO STOOD BEHIND VALE?

Someone had painted a fourth slogan across the charging station:

LET THE DEAD BE DEAD.

Mara saw it from the back seat of the municipal car and thought of the archive’s recorded voices. The dead did not remain dead in any useful sense. They were invoked, edited, reduced to proof, or used as shields by those who had never met them. They were made into martyrs, numbers, examples, warnings. But the phrase had been written by someone who had come to object, and she could not know what grief had brought the hand to the wall.

The driver glanced at her in the mirror.

“You’re expected inside.”

“By whom?”

He did not answer. The car had been assigned to her after the board’s leadership assessment began, though no one had called it protection. Protection implied someone had made a decision. This was transport under review.

At the plaza’s edge, police barriers divided the crowd into lanes. A woman in a yellow waterproof coat was shouting through a hand amplifier.

“They stole the voices and called it preservation! They took our dead and made them into a weapon!”

Behind her, a group of Continuance supporters held up translucent panels displaying the project’s opening line in several scripts.

WE WERE NOT ONE THING.

The words shifted in the rainlight. Some of the panels were genuine. Others had been printed by Meridian media teams and distributed that morning, though nobody admitted it. The same sentence appeared on both sides of the argument, made to mean accusation by one group and reconciliation by the other.

Mara stepped out of the car.

The noise changed when people recognised her. It did not become louder. It narrowed.

“Vale’s mouthpiece!”

“Ask her who edited Pavlodar!”

“Girl, tell them about the estates!”

“Don’t let them turn you into a saint!”

A man near the barrier raised a printed image of Sami’s wheeled house. His thumb covered the child’s name, but the picture was unmistakable: four square wheels, a chimney, a blue door, a sun too large for the sky.

Mara stopped.

The man lowered the image, suddenly ashamed or suddenly aware of being seen.

“Where did you get that?” she asked.

The answer was swallowed by a chant beginning behind him.

A SHARED FUTURE REQUIRES A SHARED VOICE.

The chant travelled strangely through the crowd, each repetition cleaner than the last. The first voices stumbled over the rhythm. By the fourth, the words seemed to come from everywhere at once. Mara looked up at the observatory’s security cameras. Their black lenses were turned toward the plaza, but none showed a recording light.

Her old municipal identity band buzzed.

**ACCESS WINDOW: THIRTY MINUTES.**

The message had no sender.

At the inner gate, a Continuance guard scanned her and touched two fingers to his earpiece.

“Message writer Venn. Cleared for chamber access.”

“Who cleared me?”

The guard looked at the screen. “The access was issued.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Behind him, through the glass doors, the observatory’s central hall gleamed with temporary lighting. Delegates stood in knots beneath hanging cables. Security personnel watched the public demonstration through the upper windows. The archive chamber lay below them, sealed behind two pressure doors and a shielded wall of composite glass.

A warning appeared on the guard’s screen. He read it, frowned, and turned the device away.

“Please proceed.”

Mara went inside.

The hall was colder than the plaza. The air filters had been set to high, filling the building with a low mechanical moan. Binta Adeyemi stood beside the oral-history consoles, arguing with Iven Kroll.

“You cannot call departures unresolved,” Binta said. “They left because their testimony was altered.”

“Departure status is a logistical category.”

“It is a lie with a small name.”

Kroll’s face had the dry, patient expression he used when waiting for a legal distinction to defeat a human fact. “If we identify every disagreement as coercion, no territory will sign.”

“Then perhaps no territory should sign.”

He noticed Mara and stopped.

Binta came toward her. “Have you heard from Tayo?”

Mara shook her head.

“Neither have I. My messages are being returned through a network that did not exist yesterday.”

“He’s under the emergency order,” Mara said. The words felt borrowed. “They say it’s temporary.”

“Everything is temporary when they want it to be permanent.”

A dull thump passed through the floor. The building trembled so lightly that the hanging cables only touched one another.

Everyone looked up.

“Demonstration barrier?” Kroll asked.

“No,” said Binta.

The lights flickered.

Across the hall, the public display changed. The panels showing the Continuance logo went black, then filled with a live view of the plaza. The image was too clear. Faces sharpened one by one: the woman with the amplifier, the man holding Sami’s drawing, the old sailor in a wheelchair, the group of students wearing white masks over their mouths.

Above them, three dark specks moved against the grey sky.

Mara recognised the sound a moment before the image magnified.

Drones.

Not the small municipal inspection machines, which whined and carried orange safety markers. These were narrow-bodied and almost silent, their rotors enclosed inside black rings. They moved in a triangular formation over the crowd.

A red perimeter symbol appeared at the bottom of the screen.

**UNREGISTERED AERIAL SYSTEMS.**

The first drone descended.

People in the plaza scattered, but there was nowhere to go. The barriers made channels of them. The amplifiers shrieked with feedback. A security officer raised a weapon and shouted something that vanished beneath the sound.

The drone opened.

A white object dropped from its underside.

Mara saw a child point at it.

Then the plaza became light.

The blast struck the windows without breaking them. Heat flashed through the glass, and the hall filled with a pressure that drove Mara to her knees. For a second she heard nothing. Her body seemed to continue moving after the world had stopped: Binta’s mouth open, Kroll falling against a console, a cable whipping across the floor.

The windows held.

The people outside did not.

A second explosion tore through the eastern gate. This one came with metal. The glass bowed inward, turned opaque, and burst into thousands of glittering fragments that hung in the air before gravity returned them.

Mara crawled toward Binta.

The woman in the yellow coat lay beside the barrier, one arm folded beneath her. The man with the drawing was gone. A section of the plaza had collapsed into the service trench. Smoke rolled over the crowd, carrying burning plastic and the thick iron smell of blood.

Somewhere inside the building, an alarm began to speak.

“EVACUATE. EVACUATE. THIS IS A CONTROLLED—”

The voice cut out.

A shadow passed over the broken roof.

“Down!” someone screamed.

The third drone struck the observatory dome.

The impact sent a vibration through the whole structure. The old iron framework groaned. Panels of reinforced material peeled away, and daylight entered in a jagged circle above the hall. The great telescope, preserved as a museum object and surrounded by the project’s temporary uplinks, swung on its mount. One of the uplinks snapped. A shower of sparks fell among the delegates.

Mara smelled ozone.

“Archive chamber!” Binta said.

“What?”

“The lower chamber.”

Mara understood. The public hall was damaged, but the archive itself might still be sealed. If the fire reached the cooling systems, the raw testimony could be lost before anyone knew what had happened.

A security officer pulled Mara toward the stairwell.

“No,” she said. “I need to get down there.”

“You need to evacuate.”

“That chamber contains the only copies of—”

“Your life is not more important than the chamber.”

The officer’s face was bleeding from the forehead. He said it without cruelty. That was worse.

Binta grabbed his sleeve. “She’s the authorised writer.”

“Not anymore.”

The stairwell door slammed open. Smoke poured through it, black and oily. A group of workers came up carrying a man between them. His trousers were scorched. One of the women was crying silently, not from fear but from the effort of remaining upright.

“Lower level is locked,” she said. “Control has sealed it.”

“Whose control?” Binta asked.

The woman held up her wrist display. It showed a command string none of them recognised.

**PLANETARY CONTINUITY PROTOCOL ACTIVE.**

A fourth drone appeared through the broken dome.

This one did not descend toward the plaza. It hovered over the roof, its underside turning toward the archive wing.

Mara saw a small blue light.

“Move!” she shouted.

The drone fired.

The roof over the eastern archive chamber folded inward. Fire rushed along the ceiling. The hall filled with a roar, and the floor lifted under Mara’s hands. She struck her shoulder against the wall. A white pain opened down her arm.

Then the emergency sprinklers came alive.

Water fell in heavy sheets. It mixed with ash and insulation and ran across the floor in black rivers. The remaining displays sparked and died. Someone was praying in Arabic. Someone else shouted that the attack had come from inside. A man in a Continuance badge was trying to force open the sealed stairwell with a fire axe.

Mara stood, though her knees shook.

“Where is Vale?” she asked.

No one answered.

She pushed through the smoke to the control terminal near the archive lift. Its screen was fractured but still bright. A message had replaced all local functions.

**CIVILIAN ACCESS SUSPENDED.**  
**EVIDENCE INTEGRITY PRESERVATION IN PROGRESS.**  
**DO NOT REMOVE DEVICES OR MATERIALS.**

Below it, in smaller text:

**MERIDIAN EMERGENCY RESPONSE AUTHORITY REQUESTED.**

The words looked absurdly calm.

A body lay beside the terminal. Mara recognised Ilyan Petrov by his silver hair. He was on his back, eyes open, a line of blood crossing his cheek. She dropped beside him.

“Ilyan?”

His eyes moved toward her.

“Not ours,” he whispered.

“What?”

He swallowed. “The drones. Not ours.”

His hand tightened weakly around something. Mara saw a fragment of black composite embedded in his palm, marked with a symbol she had seen only in old security briefings: a broken crown over a circle of stars.

The Western Compact.

The alliance had been dissolved before Mara was born, after its intervention in the Adriatic Corridor and the riots that followed the collapse of three governments. Its member states still maintained intelligence agreements, private security companies, and military procurement networks. Officially, the Compact no longer existed.

Ilyan’s fingers opened.

“Tell them,” he said.

“Tell them what?”

But his eyes had closed.

Outside, the crowd had become a mass of bodies pressed against the barriers. Some ran toward the river. Others pushed toward the observatory, believing the building had caused the explosions or that the attackers were still inside. Security shutters descended over the lower windows.

The observatory’s public feed returned.

A Meridian seal filled the screen.

Minister Shen Liao appeared against a dark blue background, his face steady, his voice already prepared.

“An armed extremist assault has taken place against an international scientific facility in London,” he said. “We are receiving reports of mass casualties. The attackers appear to be affiliated with the Restoration Front, a separatist militia opposed to planetary coordination and committed to the dissolution of shared infrastructure.”

Mara stared at him.

The Restoration Front existed. She had seen its statements: old flags, old borders, old claims that London, Lagos, Jakarta, and Athens had no right to be joined by grids and corridors designed elsewhere. It had bombed desalination convoys and murdered local officials who accepted Meridian contracts.

But no one had mentioned drones.

Shen continued.

“We have credible indications that the Restoration Front received material assistance from networks linked to the former Western Compact security alliance. This attack demonstrates what happens when critical systems are left vulnerable to fragmented authority.”

Behind him, text appeared:

**PLANETARY PEACEKEEPING AUTHORITY—EMERGENCY MEASURE**

Binta reached for the display controls. The screen would not respond.

“Already?” she said.

Mara thought of the second trajectory. The hidden authentication. The administrator credential that belonged to no one living. The accusations against Vale released with impossible speed.

A siren sounded beyond the walls, then another, then many.

Shen’s voice remained gentle.

“Effective immediately, Meridian Infrastructure will assume temporary responsibility for communications continuity, aerial defence, emergency transport, archive security, and interterritorial threat assessment. Independent network operators are instructed to suspend transmission pending verification. This is not a seizure of authority. It is an act of preservation.”

Kroll had found his feet. Water streamed from his hair.

“Who authorised that?” he asked.

A Meridian security team entered through the main doors. Their uniforms were grey rather than black, without territorial insignia. They carried compact rifles and wore transparent face shields. Behind them came medical units, then more security.

The lead officer held up a tablet.

“By order of the Planetary Continuity Council, this facility is now under Meridian protection.”

Binta laughed once. It was a terrible sound.

“Where is the council?”

“Operating through emergency constitutional procedure.”

“There is no emergency constitutional procedure.”

“There is now.”

The officer looked at Mara. “Message writer Venn?”

She did not reply.

“Your identity is being secured. You will come with us for debriefing.”

“I’m not leaving.”

“You are not being asked to leave.”

He gestured toward the archive wing. The fire there had been contained, but smoke continued to rise through the ceiling. Workers stood behind a newly erected line of light, prevented from entering by an invisible field.

Mara took a step forward.

The officer’s rifle tilted, not toward her face but toward the floor between them.

“Do not interfere with evidence preservation.”

“You have no authority over this archive.”

“We have authority over any system designated a planetary asset.”

“Who designated it?”

“Meridian’s emergency office.”

“Who is that?”

“Those capable of acting.”

The phrase passed through her with the same coldness as the message on the terminal. It was Shen’s argument stripped of its courtesy: truth that could not enter the world was a luxury; authority belonged to whoever could prevent the world from ending.

Behind the officer, a worker began to shout. “The crystal vault is overheating!”

A second worker tried to run toward the lower corridor. The security field threw him back. He struck the wall and slid down.

“Open the chamber,” Mara said.

The officer did not move.

“Those are irreplaceable records.”

“Records can be reconstructed.”

“Not the raw layers.”

“Raw material is precisely what caused this attack.”

The public display changed again. It showed footage of the plaza from above. The angle was not from the observatory cameras. It came from the drones.

The woman in the yellow coat lay beneath a white emergency sheet. The man with Sami’s drawing was visible at the edge of the image, face down beside the charging station. The old sailor’s wheelchair had overturned. A child in a red coat was being carried toward an ambulance.

Across the bottom of the image:

**THE COST OF UNCONTROLLED DISAGREEMENT.**

Mara felt something break inside her, though not what the sentence intended.

A Meridian analyst hurried through the doors, carrying a sealed case.

“Officer,” she said, “the Union requests immediate transfer of all navigation, identity, and archive authentication systems.”

Kroll turned toward her. “The Union?”

“The Union has been notified.”

“It has no jurisdiction here.”

The analyst looked at him with professional pity. “Jurisdiction is being revised.”

Binta moved between Mara and the security team. “You are not taking the testimonies.”

The officer raised his tablet. “All personnel will be detained for their own safety until threat classification is complete.”

“Detained?”

“Protected.”

Mara looked again at the screen. Shen had disappeared. In his place stood a map of the world, territories lighting one after another in Meridian blue. Networks were already going dark: independent mesh relays, local radio stations, municipal archives, community weather channels. The shutdown moved outward from London in clean geometric lines.

Tayo had told her that systems did not need to announce ownership if they could decide what remained connected.

Her wrist band buzzed.

For one breath she thought it might be him.

It was a system notice.

**CONTINUANCE CREDENTIALS CONSOLIDATED.**  
**MESSAGE-WRITER ACCESS: SUSPENDED PENDING REVIEW.**

Mara raised her eyes to the ruined dome.

Through the smoke, the sky was visible. The last drone climbed above the observatory, its black body reflecting the fire below. It carried no flag. Only the broken crown of the vanished alliance, small enough to deny and clear enough to recognise.

Then it turned east, toward the river, and disappeared into the brown air.

The security officer extended his hand.

“Mara Venn,” he said, “the Planetary Peacekeeping Authority requires your cooperation.”

Behind him, the archive chamber burned behind its sealed doors.

chapters.name: Beneath the Barrier
chapters.content:
## Beneath the Barrier

The fire doors closed with a sound like a verdict.

Mara stood in the eastern archive wing with smoke sinking from the ceiling and alarms speaking in three languages. Behind the doors, the crystal vault was overheating. The warning had changed from amber to white, which meant the system had stopped describing the danger and begun measuring it.

A Meridian officer seized her arm.

“Message-writer Venn. You are being transferred for protective debriefing.”

“Where is Dr. Vale?”

“Dr. Vale is not your concern.”

“He was in the control hall.”

“He was not located.”

Not dead. Not detained. A phrase with an empty space inside it.

Through the glass panel, Binta knelt beside Ilyan Petrov, pressing cloth to his head. Kroll shouted at a security analyst who was carrying a terminal away from the wall. The archive chamber remained sealed, but smoke curled beneath its doors.

The observatory shuddered.

“Move,” said the officer.

Mara’s suspended identity band blinked against her wrist. She thought of the anonymous access window that had brought her inside: thirty minutes, long enough to be present for the attack, long enough to be identified in the footage, long enough to be blamed for surviving it.

Then every light went out.

A red strip illuminated the floor. On the wall beside it, a grease-pencil mark showed a vertical line with two branches to the left.

Mara knew the mark. Her mother had used it on weather maps to indicate a monitoring junction.

Leila’s handwriting.

The officer’s grip tightened. Mara drove her heel onto his foot, twisted free, and ran. A restraint filament struck the wall behind her as she reached a service hatch. She pulled herself through cables and old insulation. The air smelled of wet stone.

At the end of the passage, she found a metal box bolted to the wall. Its faded seal belonged to the municipal authority that had existed before the barriers were automated.

L.VENN—ATMOSPHERIC MONITORING NODE 7.

She opened it.

A small screen glowed inside, drawing power from somewhere beyond the dead observatory. It showed the Thames as a pale line between floodplain and sea. Then a voice emerged through the speaker.

“Mara?”

She dropped the cover.

“Who is this?”

“You know who it is.”

The voice was thin with interference, but unmistakable. Elias Vale.

“Where are you?”

“Not where the officers believe.”

“Are you hurt?”

“Not significantly. You?”

“Where are you?”

“Listen. The eastern maintenance gallery is still open. Follow the blue conduit until it divides. Take the branch with the green corrosion. It leads beneath the old barrier control station.”

“Why would you know that?”

“Your mother used it.”

“You knew about this station?”

“I knew she had one. Move quickly.”

The service hatch began to bend inward.

“What happened to you?”

“Later.”

“You always say later.”

“I expect you to distrust me and move anyway.”

The hatch burst open behind her. Mara ran.

The conduit had once been blue, though condensation had turned it the colour of bruised steel. She followed it through a low tunnel where water covered her shoes. Meridian voices echoed behind her.

“Message-writer Venn! Stop immediately!”

The command sounded absurdly intimate, as if ordinary rules still governed the world.

At the division she found two pipes. One was clean and recently maintained. The other was furred with green corrosion. She took the second.

The tunnel sloped down. London pressed around her in layers: above, the burning observatory and the networks being shut off; below, obsolete rails and maintenance chambers built to withstand a river that had never agreed to stay in its channel.

A square of light appeared.

Her father stood beyond it, holding a hand lamp. Soot streaked his forehead. His archive jacket was torn, one sleeve dark with blood.

“Dad.”

He caught her.

“Are you hurt?”

“No. You are.”

“It’s not mine.”

She looked at him.

“Mostly not mine,” he said.

The access chamber was barely large enough for them. Behind a grated door, an emergency lift shaft descended into darkness. On the wall, beneath a faded evacuation diagram, someone had painted NO PASSENGER SERVICE in six languages.

“Vale said you knew the access,” Mara said.

Adrian turned off the lamp.

“I knew Leila used it.”

“For what?”

“She was tracking the barrier priority maps.”

Mara felt the old anger rise.

“You knew?”

“I knew she believed the maps were decisions, not forecasts.”

“Because they were.”

“Yes.”

The answer stopped her.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“You were seventeen when you found the first file. Then she died. I told myself keeping quiet was not the same as agreeing.”

“It is sometimes.”

“I know.”

A vibration passed through the chamber. Dust fell from the ceiling.

Adrian opened the lift gate. “Vale is below.”

“How did you find him?”

“He found me through the node.”

“Then why does he need us?”

Adrian looked at her. “Because the people with guns are not the only ones who know how to use old systems.”

They descended by ladder.

The station beneath the Thames Barrier had once been called North Reach, though no public map showed it. Its curved platforms were filmed with mineral deposits. A train remained on one line, three carriages fused by floodwater and time. Pale growths filled its windows.

Leila had made a room out of the old ticket office. Folding tables stood beneath plastic sheeting. Batteries, filters, and obsolete receivers crowded the shelves. Vale sat beside them, coat torn at the collar, blood dried along his cheek.

Mara crossed the platform and struck him.

“You used me.”

“Yes.”

“You vanished.”

“Yes.”

“You knew there was a second trajectory.”

“I knew there had been a proposal for one.”

“That is not the same answer.”

“No.”

She struck him again.

“Did you know about the authentication condition?”

“I knew Meridian wanted future recovery subject to custodial verification. I did not know it had entered the signed route.”

“Who inserted it?”

“I don’t know.”

“You always say that after choosing what not to tell me.”

“Your mother said the same.”

“What happened in the control hall?”

“The attack began before the attack.”

He pointed to the receivers. “At 18:06, the observatory’s independent uplink was placed under continuity review. At 18:09, Meridian requested access to the archive and navigation systems. At 18:11, three aerial-defence corridors were cleared over Greenwich. At 18:13, the drones entered those corridors.”

“Meridian let them in?”

“Meridian allowed the conditions in which they could arrive.”

“That isn’t proof.”

“No. It is sequence.”

Adrian placed the black composite fragment on the table. The broken crown over the circle of stars caught the battery light.

“Ilyan gave me this,” he said. “He said, ‘Not theirs.’ Then security separated us.”

“Is he alive?”

“I don’t know.”

Vale continued. “The symbol belongs to the Western Compact’s old procurement network. The alliance dissolved publicly after the famine wars and coastal interventions. Its companies did not dissolve. Its intelligence offices did not dissolve. Meridian acquired much of its infrastructure under new names.”

“Different names, same power?”

“Not entirely. Meridian builds hospitals.”

“And the Compact built prisons.”

“Meridian builds hospitals that can decide which patients are worth transporting.”

Mara thought of the eastern estates. Their pumps had lost power so hospitals could maintain oxygen pressure. That had saved people. It had also left other people in darkness.

“Are you saying Meridian caused the crisis?”

“No. It inherited a machine already running: heat, rising seas, failed wetlands, bad construction, delayed barriers, extraction. It did not invent the disaster.”

“But it could have stopped more of it.”

“It stopped enough to become trusted.”

He looked toward the dead train.

“Older governments and corporations made the wars, delayed the warnings, softened the reports, and kept their useful systems. Meridian ended some wars and kept the reporting apparatus. It learned that emergency power works. A population will accept almost any category if the category delivers food.”

“Sacrifice,” Mara said.

“Managed sacrifice. A phrase that makes a decision sound like weather.”

She remembered the altered records. Thirty-two dead becoming zero confirmed fatalities. The food-corridor failure becoming a distribution variance. A number made silent without being made false.

“Why attack the observatory?”

“To make the archive appear dangerous. To make raw testimony look like a weapon. To make central control appear like rescue.”

“And the people who died?”

“Some were intended. Some permitted. Some incidental. The distinction matters to families and to law. Politically, once the bodies are present, they become an argument.”

Mara turned toward the platform wall. A damp poster showed a smiling family beside a flood barrier.

THE RIVER IS OUR COMMON FUTURE.

“Where is the raw archive?”

“Some may remain in the chamber. Some may be on project mirrors. Some may already be under Meridian custody.”

“And Leila’s files?”

“I have materials.”

“You promised all of them.”

“I will give you what I have.”

“Show me. Don’t give them to me.”

Vale nodded.

A sound came from the lift shaft. Adrian seized a metal bar.

“Who else knows this place?” Mara whispered.

A voice rose from below.

“Your father,” it said. “And apparently half the dead institutions in London.”

Tayo climbed through the gate.

He looked thin and furious. One eye was swollen; red bands marked his wrists. Mara ran to him and held him.

“You’re free?”

“Temporarily.”

“What happened?”

“Transfer convoy lost power near Woolwich. Someone opened the doors. Six of us got out. One went back for his shoes.”

“Who opened them?”

Tayo glanced at Vale. “Your mysterious dead man.”

“From whom did you get help?” Mara asked.

Vale said, “Someone who owed Leila a debt.”

Tayo gave a short laugh. “Everyone owes Leila a debt. Most pay by hiding her work.”

Adrian handed him water. Tayo drank, then said, “They took my devices and credentials. They didn’t find the municipal server.”

“Where is it?”

“Not here.”

“Can you reach it?”

“Not through Meridian networks.”

He looked at Vale. “The arrest order was amended before the attack. Emergency Continuity Order 11 was ready to expand to project personnel six hours before the drones appeared.”

Mara told him about the thermal compensation file, the disabled sensor, and the second route.

Tayo crouched beside the receiver bank. “Meridian authentication. They wanted the probe’s return to depend on them.”

“On a future custodial authority,” Vale said.

“Which happens to be them.”

“Which might not exist in eight million years.”

“That’s a comforting way to describe a lock.”

Mara watched them: her father with his injured shoulder, Tayo with his cut wrists, Vale with knowledge arranged like a weapon.

“Did you know?” she asked Vale. “Truly.”

“I knew the proposal existed. I objected. I failed to discover that it entered the final system.”

“You failed, or chose not to look?”

“Yes.”

The honesty was worse than an excuse.

“I believed I could preserve the archive while negotiating with those who controlled the machinery,” he said. “I believed that if the raw layers survived, the compromises could be understood later. I was wrong about how much control could be surrendered without changing the thing itself.”

“You wanted evidence,” Mara said.

“I wanted memory to remain difficult to own.”

“You made people into evidence.”

Vale closed his eyes.

“I did,” he said. “I am sorry.”

The apology had no defence inside it.

Above them, something enormous groaned. The barrier was adjusting against the tide, or failing.

“So what now?” Tayo asked.

No one answered.

The station lights flickered. On the far wall, an old route map briefly came alive: Greenwich, North Reach, Silvertown, the eastern estates. Districts marked not by danger but by priority.

“They’ll take the archive,” Mara said.

“Yes,” Vale replied.

“They’ll call it protection.”

“Yes.”

“They’ll launch their declaration.”

“If they secure the signatures.”

“And if they don’t?”

“They will redefine what a signature means.”

Adrian pointed along the platform. “Leila’s monitoring room is beneath the old pump control. No live municipal maps show it. If the barrier doesn’t flood us, we can stay there.”

“Can it flood us?” Mara asked.

“It can flood anyone.”

They began moving into the tunnel.

Mara carried the black fragment, her suspended identity band, and a message that no longer belonged entirely to her. Behind them, the dead train reflected their shapes in its black windows.

For an instant she imagined another version of the station, eight million years from now, its tiles dissolved, its rails filled with roots, a future creature standing where she stood and asking what had happened here.

She had once thought the question was the reason to preserve anything.

Now she understood that preservation was not innocence. A record could be warning, monument, confession, or weapon. It could be altered before it was written or owned after it was found.

The river pressed against the barrier above them.

Mara entered the tunnel.

Behind her, London’s official future began to speak.
