Water struck metal.

Something moved in a sealed chamber, or something remembered movement. A child laughed, impossibly close and impossibly far away.

Nara waited.

Mara’s voice emerged worn by distance and repetition. It was younger than the voice that had spoken through the open archive, but not young. There was a scar in its rhythm, a hesitation that had survived every conversion.

“You are not required to forgive us.”

The marsh breathed around her.

“You are not required to hate us.”

A flock passed overhead, their conductive filaments flashing blue.

“You are not required to restore what we were.”

Nara had heard these words many times. She had heard them in the first chamber, with water around her knees and Seraphel’s relay trying to crush them into a single authorised meaning. She had heard them translated into tide-count, scent, percussion, and the hand-sign language of the Veldt.

But here, at the former launch platform, she heard what the words did not ask.

They did not ask to be admired for their honesty.

They did not ask to be used as a warning that made the living obedient.

They did not even ask to be remembered correctly. That, Nara now understood, was impossible. Every remembering was a meeting between what had happened and what the listener needed not to repeat.

Mara continued.

“You are not required to become what we imagined.”

Nara looked down at the water. Beneath the surface, the foundations of London extended in broken lines. A road passed under the marsh and emerged nowhere. A tower leaned among the roots. Fish moved through the rooms where people had once slept.

“Let the old world end,” Mara said.

The recording ended with a soft mechanical click.

For a long time, Nara did not move.

The first time she had heard the sentence, she had thought it was a command to destroy. Later she had understood it as refusal: refusal of restoration, refusal of destiny, refusal of the comforting belief that survival entitled anyone to rule.

Now, with the reeds bending around her and the drowned city holding its broken shapes below, she heard another possibility.

The old world could end without the past being excused.

It could end without being erased.

Nara placed the bowl of estuary water on the black stone. The surface trembled. Somewhere beneath the platform, a root had found a seam in the foundation and entered it. The reed growing there was taller than the others, its leaves silver underneath.

“The future has not forgiven you,” Nara said.

The words entered the case and were recorded by the open channel.

She paused, aware of the danger in speaking for everyone who had come after. The old species had done that constantly. A minister spoke for the hungry. A council spoke for the displaced. A House spoke for descendants. A Keeper spoke for the archive. Each time, a multitude had been made into one voice and then made responsible for what that voice demanded.

So Nara corrected herself.

“I have not forgiven you,” she said. “Not because forgiveness is impossible. Because it is not mine to grant on behalf of those you harmed.”

The marsh received the sentence without answering.

“But I have accepted responsibility for what I do with what you left.”

She touched the reed fibre.

“I will not restore you as destiny. I will not destroy you to make myself pure. I will study your tools, where study does not become possession. I will preserve your names, where names can be found. I will preserve the gaps where they cannot. I will teach those who come after me that rescue does not erase coercion, and beauty does not cancel harm, and failure does not make every attempt worthless.”

Her voice shook. She let it shake.

“I will not make a single virtue from your survival. I will not make a single guilt from your existence.”

The case recorded her separately from Mara.

SOURCE ACCOUNT RETAINED.

Nara smiled at the old machine’s stubbornness.

“Good,” she said.

At the edge of the platform, a new shoot unfolded. Its stem was red at the base and green at the tip. Tiny pale flowers opened along it, each one carrying enough salt to glitter in the morning light. The roots below were already crossing the buried rooms, binding brick to mineral, wire to mud, old barrier to living wetland.

No one had planned what the marsh would become.

People had altered it, abandoned it, studied it, poisoned it, and tried to make it obey. The reeds had taken those conditions and made a life that was not a return.

Nara closed the memory case.

Far out over the estuary, the sky species turned as one body. Their shadows moved across the water, across the towers, across the launch platform and the reeds spreading through the ruins.

The archive remained open.

The dead remained unable to make meaning for the living.

The living, imperfectly and without permission from the past, continued.
